A Swedish employee has 25 days of holiday a year under the Annual Leave Act ([Svensk Handel](https://svenskhandel.se/arbetsgivarguiden/information-in-english/vacation/the-right-to-vacation)). Norway also has 25 working days, counting Saturdays, which makes four weeks and one day ([Arbeidstilsynet](https://arbeidstilsynet.no/en/working-conditions/holiday)). Denmark has 25 days earned at 2.08 days a month ([IDA](https://ida.dk/en/career-and-legal-advice/holiday-and-time-off/use-your-holidays)). Finland accrues two days a month, rising to 2.5 after a full year ([SAK](https://www.sak.fi/en/working-life/ground-rules-working/holidays-and-holiday-pay)).

Then someone tells you that Italian law gives four weeks. It sounds like a step down. In practice the gap is smaller than the statute suggests, and the structure is different enough that your Nordic holiday policy will not fit as it is.

## The Italian building blocks

Italy does not have one holiday bank. The law and the national collective agreement (CCNL) create separate entitlements:

- **Annual holiday (ferie).** At least four weeks a year by law. Part of it must be taken in the year it accrues, and that part cannot be replaced by cash while employment continues. The CCNL may give more.
- **Paid hours off (ROL and ex-holiday permits).** Many CCNLs add a block of paid hours each year, tracked separately. Employees use them for half days, appointments or bridges between holidays.
- **Public holidays.** Twelve national holidays plus the local patron saint's day. They do not count against holiday.
- **Sick leave.** A separate category with its own rules, never drawn from holiday.
- **Family leave.** Maternity, paternity and parental leave are protected by statute.

Put the first two together and many Italian employees end up with time off close to the Nordic norm. How close depends on the CCNL and on seniority.

## Where Nordic habits collide

**Holiday pay works differently.** Nordic systems compute holiday pay or a holiday supplement as a percentage of earnings. In Italy, the employee simply keeps receiving normal pay while on holiday. There is no separate holiday supplement by law. Do not build one into an Italian offer by habit, or your cost model will double count.

**Saving days.** Nordic employees are used to rules on carrying days forward. Italian rules on what must be used in the year and what can be carried are set by law and the CCNL. Unused leave is a liability that grows, and it is paid out at exit.

**Unlimited holiday.** Some Nordic scale-ups offer "take what you need". In Italy this does not work: without tracking you cannot show that the legal minimum was taken.

**Approval.** In Italy, as at home, the employer has a say on when holiday is taken, within the rules on notice and timing. It does not decide whether. Treat holiday as planned capacity, not a favour.

## Summer: July at home, August in Italy

Nordic companies slow down in July. Many Italian companies, and their customers and suppliers, slow down in August, with a peak around 15 August. If your Italian sales lead or field engineer serves Italian accounts, plan for their holiday to fall in August, not July. That gives you useful coverage: Italians working while Stockholm is on holiday, and the reverse a month later.

## Budget and records

The cost of an Italian employee includes paid time not worked: holiday, hours off, public holidays. A model that only uses salary per working day will understate the cost per hour. That is normal and predictable once it is in the plan.

Keep three things in place:

1. A record of holiday and hours off accrued and taken, per employee.
2. A shared calendar that shows Italian and Nordic public holidays side by side.
3. Offer letters and handbooks that describe Italian entitlements in Italian terms, not by copying the Swedish policy.

## How we handle it

As Employer of Record (EOR) we apply the CCNL entitlements, track the balances and treat each category correctly in payroll. You approve the planning. Every month you see the balances in the payroll summary.

## Questions we hear from Nordic companies

**Can we give Italian staff 25 days to match the Nordic office?**
Yes. The law and the CCNL are floors. Many Nordic companies harmonise holiday across countries. Write it into the contract, and remember that CCNL hours off still apply on top unless the contract says how they combine.

**Can unused holiday be paid out instead of taken?**
Not for the statutory part during employment. It must be taken. Unused leave is paid out only at the end of employment.

For the full set of differences, see [Italy vs Sweden](/italy-vs-sweden.html). For the cost of paid time off in a specific role, try the [cost calculator](/calculator.html).

Nordic machinery companies sell into Italy, buy from Italy and compete with Italian machine builders. Packaging, food and dairy processing, pulp and paper, automation and materials handling are all areas where Nordic and Emilian industry overlap. Bologna sits at the centre of that region.

## The region

The area around Bologna, Modena, Reggio Emilia and Parma is known for:

- packaging and automatic machinery, the "Packaging Valley";
- motorcycles and sports cars;
- mechatronics and industrial automation;
- food processing;
- logistics;
- high-performance computing around the Tecnopolo and CINECA.

Talent comes from the Università di Bologna, one of Italy's largest, for engineering, computer science, economics and agriculture, and from nearby universities in Modena, Reggio Emilia, Ferrara and Parma, which add mechanical and automotive engineers.

## Roles Nordic companies hire

- **Field service engineers** installing and maintaining equipment at Italian customers.
- **Applications engineers** supporting sales with line design and trials.
- **Supplier quality engineers** for components bought from Italian machine shops.
- **Project managers** for installations and upgrades.
- **Spare parts and service sales.**

Most of these roles are customer-facing in Italian, and many need a car and frequent travel.

## Local income tax

Bologna has a flat city surcharge of 0.8% with an exemption threshold of €15,000 (pmi.it, 730/2026 table, secondary source). The Emilia-Romagna regional surcharge starts at 1.33% up to €15,000; the higher brackets still need checking against official tables. For the same gross, take-home pay in Bologna is close to Milan and above Rome and Naples.

## The contract

Machinery roles are normally under the Metalworking agreement (CCNL Metalmeccanico industria). It regulates travel allowances, how travel time counts, shift premiums and on-call work in detail, and includes a supplementary health fund.

## Practical points

- **Car and van.** Service engineers usually have a company vehicle, fuel card and tolls, managed as benefits.
- **Travel time and allowances.** Priced into the role from the start.
- **Safety.** Risk assessment, training and health checks before the first customer site.
- **INAIL.** Field roles have a higher injury premium than office roles.
- **Postings.** Installations in other EU countries need a posting notification; trips to your factory in Sweden or Finland for training are business travel.
- **Commuting.** Many factories are outside the city; a car or company shuttle is often needed.

## Why not hire in Sweden and fly in?

Italian customers expect service in Italian, on short notice, from someone who knows local practice. Flying engineers in from the Nordics is expensive and slow. A local engineer employed through an EOR gives you presence without an Italian company.

## Hiring without an entity

With an Employer of Record (EOR), we employ the engineer under the Metalworking CCNL, handle travel expenses on actuals and run payroll. You manage the service organisation. Cost: employment cost plus €250 a month, invoiced in SEK, NOK, DKK or EUR.

## Questions we hear from Nordic companies

**Do we need an Italian company to install machines at Italian customers?**
Not for employing the engineer. The employment sits with the EOR. Whether your sales and installation contracts need a local entity is a separate commercial and tax question, which you should check with your adviser, especially if the engineer also sells.

**Can the engineer work on customer sites in other EU countries?**
Yes. Short trips are business travel. Longer assignments are postings and need a prior notification in the destination country, which we file. Social security normally stays in Italy during a posting.

**How do we handle on-call and weekend service?**
The Metalworking CCNL regulates on-call duty, overtime and weekend work in detail. Define the service pattern before the offer, so that it can be priced and written into the contract. Surprises here are the most common source of disputes in field service.

**Is a company car taxable for the engineer?**
If it is also used privately, yes, as a benefit calculated on a flat share of a standard cost that depends on emissions. A van used only for work is a work tool.

## In short

Emilia-Romagna gives Nordic machinery companies engineers who know the customers, the suppliers and the competitors. Hire them locally, under the Metalworking CCNL, with travel, car and on-call rules written in from day one. Keep sales authority clear if the engineer also sells. Price the role on its full cost, including allowances and INAIL for field work, and use the EOR until the Italian business is large enough for its own company.

See the [Bologna city page](/hire-in-bologna.html) and [industrial engineers in Italy](/hire-engineers-manufacturing-italy.html). Estimate the cost in the [calculator](/calculator.html).

It is a familiar story in Nordic tech and design companies. Two years ago you hired an Italian developer or product specialist as a consultant. They invoice monthly on a VAT number. Today they attend every stand-up, have a company email, report to a team lead and work only for you.

On paper, a consultant. In practice, an employee. Italian authorities look at practice.

## Why it is a risk

If a person works only for you, on your schedule, with your tools and under your direction, the relationship can be reclassified as employment. The consequences fall on the company:

- contributions that should have been paid, with penalties and interest;
- tax withholding that should have been made;
- employee entitlements the person never received, such as the 13th month, holiday and TFR;
- weaker position in any dispute.

The longer it runs, the larger the exposure.

There is also a people risk. A consultant has no paid holiday, no sick pay and no social protection beyond what they pay for themselves. Good people eventually take a permanent job elsewhere.

## Signs that it is time

- The person works only or mainly for you.
- They have fixed hours or are expected online during core hours.
- They use your equipment and accounts.
- They manage or are managed like staff.
- The engagement has no defined end or deliverable.

Two or three of these together are enough to act.

## How conversion works with an EOR

1. **Agree the terms.** Salary as RAL (annual gross), start date, role. The consultant's daily rate is not the right reference: as an employee they lose some costs and gain protections and benefits. We help you translate one into the other.
2. **Choose the CCNL and level.** Based on the job and your sector.
3. **Draft the contract.** In Italian with an English version, with IP assignment, confidentiality and, if needed, a lavoro agile agreement.
4. **Register and start.** We handle the registrations and the first payroll.
5. **Close the consultancy.** The VAT number arrangement ends cleanly, with a final invoice.

The usual timeline is about 30 days.

## What changes in cost

For you, the monthly invoice from the consultant becomes the employment cost plus our fee: gross salary, employer contributions, INAIL, TFR, plus €250 a month. For the person, net income changes depending on their previous tax regime. Some flat-rate freelancers paid little tax; make sure the candidate understands the net figure before signing. The [net pay calculator](/net-pay-calculator.html) is a good starting point.

## Probation and seniority

A probation period in the new contract is possible but delicate for someone who has already worked with you for years. Discuss it openly. The past consultancy does not automatically count as seniority, but it does count as evidence if there is ever a dispute about the earlier relationship. That is one more reason to convert sooner rather than later.

## Several consultants?

The same process applies to a group. We also move employees from other EOR providers on the same timeline.

## Questions we hear from Nordic companies

**Will the person earn less as an employee?**
Gross may look lower than the daily rate, but as an employee they gain paid holiday, sick pay, the 13th month, the TFR and social protection, and they stop paying their own contributions. Compare net income and protections, not daily rate against salary.

**Does conversion admit that the past arrangement was wrong?**
Conversion changes the future relationship. It does not by itself settle the past. If the arrangement ran for a long time, discuss the history with an adviser; converting sooner reduces the period at risk.

**Can we keep paying them as a freelancer for part of their work?**
Generally not for the same work. Mixing employment and freelance invoicing for the same tasks invites reclassification of both.

## In short

If an Italian consultant works only for you, in your team and on your schedule, treat it as employment before someone else does. Agree a RAL, choose the CCNL and level, write IP and remote terms into the contract, and close the consultancy cleanly. The conversion takes about a month through an EOR. It reduces risk for you and gives the person the protection they have been missing, which is usually what keeps good people.

For the alternatives, see [EOR, own company or freelancers](/italy-eor-vs-entity.html). Price the conversion in the [cost calculator](/calculator.html).

When a Nordic company budgets an Italian hire, the first question is usually: how much does a euro of gross salary cost us? The answer depends on where you are coming from.

- In **Sweden**, employer contributions are 31.42% of gross pay in 2026 ([Skatteverket](https://www.skatteverket.se/servicelankar/otherlanguages/englishengelska/businessesandemployers.4.2fb39afe18dabf1e4d24a3d.html)).
- In **Norway**, employer's national insurance contributions are 14.1% in zone I in 2026 ([Skatteetaten](https://www.skatteetaten.no/en/rates/employers-national-insurance-contributions/?year=2026)).
- In **Italy**, employer social contributions are roughly 30% of gross pay, depending on sector, size and role, plus INAIL injury insurance and the TFR accrual.

So a Swedish CFO will find the Italian contribution rate familiar. A Norwegian CFO will find it about double. Danish and Finnish models are structured differently again, so compare total employer cost, not one rate.

## Three layers, compared

Every system has the same three layers on a gross salary:

1. contributions paid by the employer on top of gross;
2. contributions withheld from the employee's gross;
3. income tax withheld from the employee.

What differs is the weight of each.

### Employer side in Italy

The largest part is the pension contribution (IVS) to INPS: **23.81%** of taxable pay for the employer. On top come unemployment, sickness and maternity, family allowances and guarantee funds, which bring the total to around 30%. INAIL injury insurance is separate and depends on the risk class: well under 1% for office roles, more for technical and production roles.

Then two Italian items with no direct Nordic equivalent: the **13th month** (and a 14th under some CCNLs), which carries contributions like any salary, and the **TFR** at 6.91% of pay a year.

### Employee side in Italy

The employee's IVS contribution is **9.19%** of taxable pay, withheld by the employer. The rate rises by one point on pay above €56,224 a year.

The employee sees this contribution on the payslip, and it reduces the income on which tax is calculated.

### Income tax: IRPEF

Italian national income tax is progressive in three bands:

- 23% up to €28,000;
- 33% from €28,000 to €50,000;
- 43% above €50,000.

Each band applies only to its slice of income. Employment tax credits reduce the result, mainly on lower salaries. Regional and municipal surcharges come on top, but they are small compared with Swedish municipal tax: from 1.23% to about 3.33% regional and 0% to 1.2% municipal, depending on the city.

The figures above come from professional secondary sources. We confirm them for each specific offer.

## Side by side

| Item | Italy | Sweden |
|---|---|---|
| Employer contributions | About 30%, with IVS 23.81% | 31.42% |
| Extra employer lines | 13th (and 14th) month, TFR 6.91%, INAIL | Occupational pension via agreement |
| Employee contribution | 9.19% IVS, withheld | Handled through the Swedish tax and pension system |
| Income tax | IRPEF 23/33/43% plus small local surcharges | Municipal and state income tax |
| Health care | National health service, tax-funded | Public, tax-funded |

## What this means for an offer

**Compare total cost, not gross.** A Swedish salary converted at the exchange rate tells you little. Compare the full employer cost of the Italian role with the full employer cost at home.

**Expect the candidate to ask about net.** Italian candidates compare offers on monthly take-home pay. Be ready with a net figure for their city. The [net pay calculator](/net-pay-calculator.html) gives a first estimate.

**Expect variation.** CCNL, sector and contract type all move the employer cost. A single percentage is a starting point, not a quote.

## Questions we hear from Nordic companies

**Is the Italian rate the same for every role?**
No. Sector, company size, contract type and the CCNL all move it, and INAIL depends on the risk class of the job. That is why we quote per role rather than with one percentage.

**Do Italian contributions stop at a ceiling, like some Nordic caps?**
For employees first insured from 1996 onwards, pension contributions stop above a yearly ceiling, €122,295 in 2026. Below that, contributions apply to all taxable pay.

**Do we also pay Italian corporate tax because we employ someone?**
Employment through an EOR does not by itself make your company taxable in Italy. What the employee does can matter, especially in sales. See our article on permanent establishment risk.

Put a real salary into the [cost calculator](/calculator.html), or read the full [Italy vs Sweden](/italy-vs-sweden.html) comparison.

A Nordic company that wants people in Italy has three practical options. Which one fits depends on how many people, for how long, and whether they will sell in your name.

## Route 1: freelancers

The Italian freelancer invoices on a VAT number (partita IVA). It is fast and requires nothing from you in Italy.

It fits short, clearly defined projects with real independence: the freelancer has other clients, decides how and when to work, and delivers a result.

It does not fit a person who works only for you, full time, on your schedule, with your tools and in your team. Italian authorities can reclassify that as employment. You then owe the contributions and tax that should have been paid, plus penalties. Many Nordic companies drift into this situation: a consultant who became "one of the team" over two years.

## Route 2: your own Italian company

An Italian srl (limited company) or a branch makes you the employer directly. It fits stable teams, local sales and a long-term commitment.

What it involves: incorporation, a bank account, registrations with the tax agency, INPS and INAIL, payroll, statutory accounts, an accountant and annual filings. It takes months to set up and creates fixed costs that remain if plans change. A branch or subsidiary is also the clear answer when Italian staff conclude contracts for you.

## Route 3: Employer of Record

An Employer of Record (EOR) employs the person on your behalf. We hold the Italian contract under the right CCNL, run payroll and filings, and you direct the work.

It fits first hires, market tests and small distributed teams. Start-up time is days for EU and EEA citizens. There is nothing to register in Italy, and the cost is the employment cost plus a flat fee: €250 per employee per month with us, invoiced in SEK, NOK, DKK or EUR.

## Side by side

| | EOR | Own srl or branch | Freelancer |
|---|---|---|---|
| Time to start | Days | Months | Days |
| Legal employer | EOR | Your company | None |
| Your obligations in Italy | None | Payroll, filings, accounts | Keeping it genuinely independent |
| Main risk | Low | Fixed costs | Reclassification |
| Monthly cost | Employment cost + fee | Employment cost + local admin | Invoice |

## A common path

Many Nordic companies follow the same sequence:

1. A freelancer or two to test the market.
2. Conversion to employment through an EOR once the work becomes ongoing.
3. An Italian company when the team is large and stable or local sales require it, with the employees transferred without losing seniority.

Each step is reversible except the last, which is why it usually comes last.

## Questions to ask yourself

- Will the person work only for us? Then not a freelancer.
- Will they sign contracts with Italian customers in our name? Discuss permanent establishment before choosing.
- How many people in 18 months? One to five usually means EOR; a larger, stable team points to an entity.
- How certain is the plan? Uncertainty favours a route without fixed costs.

## Questions we hear from Nordic companies

**How long does an Italian srl take to set up?**
Months rather than weeks: incorporation, bank account, tax, INPS and INAIL registrations, and a payroll provider. Plan the timeline before you promise a start date to candidates.

**Can we start with an EOR and switch later?**
Yes. Employees move to your company without losing seniority, and the CCNL and level normally stay the same. Many Nordic companies follow exactly this path.

**Is an EOR more expensive than our own company?**
For a small team, usually not once you count local accounting, payroll, filings and management time. For a large stable team, an entity becomes more efficient. Compare total cost over two or three years.

## In short

Freelancers fit short, independent projects. An EOR fits the first hires and small teams, with no set-up and a flat fee. Your own company fits a large, stable team or a business that sells locally. Most Nordic companies move through these stages in order. The mistake to avoid is staying too long in the first stage, when the freelancer has quietly become an employee.

For a detailed comparison, see [EOR, own company or freelancers](/italy-eor-vs-entity.html). For the cost of the EOR route, use the [cost calculator](/calculator.html).

content: Swedish employers know that the open-ended contract is the default and that fixed-term forms are limited. Special fixed-term and substitute employment are each capped at 12 months within a five-year period before they convert to indefinite employment ([Business Sweden](https://www.business-sweden.com/497a82/contentassets/582cb98533254f61bce11da9af436cf8/2026/employing-staff---contracts-and-conditions-2026.pdf)). Italy follows the same philosophy. The permanent contract is the standard form, and fixed-term work is the exception with rules. The instinct you have from home is right. The specific limits are different, and a mistake has the same consequence: conversion into a permanent contract. ## What a fixed-term contract gives you An end date. When the term ends, the relationship ends, without the reasons and procedure needed to dismiss a permanent employee. That is the real benefit, and it is narrower than many founders hope: - there is a cap on total duration; - renewals and extensions are limited; - beyond an initial period, a documented reason is generally required; - breaking the rules can convert the contract into a permanent one; - fixed-term employees have the same core rights as permanent staff. The limits change from time to time. We check the current rules for each case. ## What a permanent contract gives you Retention and a cleaner offer. Italian candidates value stability highly; a permanent contract from a foreign company with no Italian office already needs some trust. Offering a fixed term on top can make a strong candidate choose a local employer. And the probation period of up to about six months, set by the CCNL, gives you a real window to assess fit. Ended correctly, it is the simplest exit there is. ## When fixed-term fits - **Replacing someone on leave.** Parental leave is the classic case, and Nordic companies will use it often. - **A defined project** with a clear end, such as a product launch or a trial programme. - **Seasonal peaks**, for example around trade fairs or fashion weeks. - **Market tests**, with care: if the test succeeds, plan the conversion to permanent in time. ## When it backfires - Using a fixed term "to be safe" for a role you expect to keep. You lose candidates and gain little. - Renewing again and again. Conversion risk grows with every renewal. - Treating fixed-term staff as a cheaper tier. Pay, leave and protections are the same. ## Cost A fixed-term contract does not save money. Pay, contributions, 13th month and TFR are the same. Fixed-term contracts can also carry an additional employer contribution [confirm current rate]. We show it in the quote. ## Part-time as an alternative If the uncertainty is about workload rather than duration, part-time may be better. Italian part-time contracts are simple, and hours can be increased later with a written amendment. ## Decision in three questions 1. Do you expect the role to exist in two years? Then permanent, with a well-used probation period. 2. Is there a specific, documentable reason for an end date? Then fixed-term may fit. 3. Is the uncertainty about hours? Then consider part-time. As Employer of Record (EOR), we draft either contract under the right CCNL and track end dates and renewals so nothing converts by accident. ## Questions we hear from Nordic companies **Can we convert a fixed-term contract to permanent early?** Yes, and it is often the best outcome. A written amendment converts it, and the time already worked counts for seniority. **Does a fixed-term employee get a probation period?** A probation period can be agreed in a fixed-term contract too, proportionate to the length of the contract and within the CCNL limits. **What if a parental-leave replacement turns out to be excellent?** Plan ahead. When the employee on leave returns, the replacement contract ends on its terms. If you want to keep the replacement, offer a new permanent role before the end date. ## In short Use permanent contracts for roles you expect to keep, and rely on a well-run probation period to manage the risk. Use fixed-term contracts where there is a real reason for an end date, such as cover for parental leave or a defined project, and track renewals closely. In Italy, as in Sweden, a fixed-term contract used out of caution tends to cost you good candidates without giving much real flexibility in return. For the wider comparison see [Italy vs Sweden](/italy-vs-sweden.html). To price either option, use the [cost calculator](/calculator.html).

content:
Nordic management has a reputation, and mostly a deserved one: flat structures, consensus, low status distance, a preference for understatement, and trust that people will take initiative. Italian professionals who join a Nordic company often like it a lot. They also find parts of it confusing.

These are generalisations, and individuals vary. But a few patterns come up often enough to plan for.

## Where the styles differ

**Hierarchy.** Italian workplaces are traditionally more hierarchical. Titles matter more, and many employees expect the manager to decide. When a Nordic manager says "what do you think we should do?", an Italian employee may hear uncertainty, or a test.

**Decisions.** Nordic teams often reach decisions through discussion until everyone is on board, sometimes without a clear moment of decision. Italian colleagues may leave the meeting unsure whether anything was decided.

**Feedback.** Nordic feedback is often direct and sparse. Italian feedback culture can be more expressive and more relational. An Italian employee who hears only short written comments may read them as dissatisfaction. Equally, a frank Italian reaction in a meeting is rarely as dramatic as it sounds to a Finnish ear.

**Relationship before task.** Italians often invest more in personal contact: a call instead of a message, a coffee before the agenda, interest in family and life. This is not small talk to be minimised; it builds the trust that makes the work go faster.

**Formality in writing.** Italian business writing can be more formal than Nordic writing, especially with customers and authorities. Inside your team, informal is fine; with Italian customers, follow your Italian colleague's lead.

## Habits that work

**Make decisions visible.** End meetings with a short written summary: what was decided, who does what, by when. It costs two minutes and removes most misunderstanding.

**Invite input, then decide.** Keep the Nordic consultation, but close it explicitly: "Thanks, I've heard the views; this is what we'll do."

**Give context with feedback.** Say what went well and why, not only what to fix. In one-to-ones, ask how the person prefers feedback.

**Use video, not only chat.** For remote Italian employees, regular video calls do more than any amount of Slack.

**Explain the flat structure.** Tell new Italian hires explicitly that you expect initiative and disagreement, and that challenging a manager is welcome. Many will need time and evidence before they believe it.

**Meet in person.** A visit to Stockholm or Copenhagen in the first months, and a visit to Italy by the manager, are worth far more than their cost.

## What Italians bring

Italian colleagues often bring strengths that complement Nordic teams: relationship building with customers and suppliers, improvisation when plans fail, and a strong sense of quality and craft. A mixed team that uses both sets of strengths is better than either alone.

## Formal frame, informal culture

One thing does not change with culture: the Italian employment relationship is formal. Contract changes, warnings, role changes and remote-work terms need writing. A relaxed team culture works well on top of that frame, not instead of it.

As Employer of Record (EOR), we handle the formal frame. You build the team.

## Questions we hear from Nordic companies

**Should we use titles with Italian colleagues?**
Inside your team, first names are fine and quickly adopted. With Italian customers and authorities, follow local practice, which can include professional titles such as Dottore or Ingegnere.

**How do we give critical feedback?**
Privately, specifically, and with context. Combine it with what works well. In writing, avoid sarcasm and understatement that can be misread across languages.

**What about language?**
English works for most professional teams. Learning a few Italian phrases, and showing interest in Italian customers in their language, is appreciated far beyond its effort.

## In short

Keep the Nordic strengths, consultation, trust and autonomy, but make decisions and priorities explicit and written. Invest in personal contact, especially with remote Italian colleagues, and give feedback with context. Explain your flat structure to new hires, and give them time to test it. On the formal side, follow the Italian frame: contracts, changes and warnings in writing.

For the formal side, see [Contracts, leave and exits](/italy-employment-contracts.html). For a first hire, start with the [cost calculator](/calculator.html).

content:
If you run a company in Sweden, you already work inside a collective bargaining model. Pay floors, working time, occupational pension and insurance usually come from an agreement between a union and an employer organisation, not from law. Sweden has no statutory minimum wage, and agreements cover close to 90% of employees, according to the [National Mediation Office](https://www.mi.se/app/uploads/the-swedish-model-and-collective-agreements.pdf).

So when an Italian adviser tells you that "every job sits under a CCNL", it sounds familiar. It mostly is. But the small differences are the ones that cause wrong offers and payroll corrections later.

## What a CCNL is

CCNL stands for Contratto Collettivo Nazionale di Lavoro, the national collective labour agreement. Employer associations and trade unions negotiate one for each sector: commerce and services, metalworking, chemicals and pharma, textiles, logistics, hospitality and many more.

Like a Swedish agreement, it is not law. It is a negotiated text. In practice it is the reference for pay and conditions in its sector, and Italian courts and inspectors treat it that way.

A CCNL typically sets:

- job classification and levels;
- minimum pay for each level;
- normal working hours and overtime rules;
- paid leave, extra hours off and public holidays;
- probation length and notice periods;
- how sick pay is topped up;
- extra monthly payments such as the 13th and 14th month;
- training, union rights and sector funds for health and pension.

## The difference that matters: there is no opt-out

In Sweden, an employer that has not signed an agreement, directly or through an employer organisation, is in principle not bound by one. There is no legislation extending agreements to everybody. Many small foreign-owned companies operate that way for a while, and set pay and terms themselves.

In Italy you should not plan on that. The working assumption for any employer, small or large, foreign or local, is that the role is placed under the CCNL that fits the sector and the job, and that pay and conditions respect it. An Italian employee who is paid below the CCNL floor can claim the difference, and the claim grows month by month. Inspectors and courts look at the CCNL first.

So the question is never "do we have an agreement?" It is "which CCNL, and which level?"

## Choosing the agreement and the level

The CCNL follows the sector of the business and the nature of the work. It is not a menu where you take the cheapest option. A software company and a retail chain will not land on the same agreement, even when both hire an accountant.

Inside the agreement, the level drives the minimum pay and many linked terms. A junior analyst and a senior manager can sit under the same CCNL at very different levels. Promotions often mean a change of level, and with it a new minimum.

Some sectors have more than one agreement signed by different organisations. Picking between them needs care, because the choice affects cost for years.

## A floor, not a ceiling

As in Sweden, the agreement sets minimums. You can always offer more, and in competitive roles you will. You cannot offer less on any point the CCNL covers.

That has direct effects:

- **Salary.** The offer must be at or above the minimum for the level. Most skilled hires are paid above it, as "superminimo".
- **Cost.** The CCNL adds items Swedish finance teams do not expect: a 13th month in every agreement, a 14th in some, extra paid hours off, and contributions to sector funds.
- **Exit.** Notice comes from the CCNL, not from statute as it does under LAS.
- **Disputes.** The CCNL is the first document a judge reads.

## What carries over from your Swedish experience

Quite a lot. You already accept that a third-party document shapes the employment relationship. You already expect a pension and insurance layer on top of salary. You already know that local unions may have a role. Italian HR people will find you easier to work with than a manager from a system without bargaining.

What does not carry over is the assumption that terms can be negotiated freely with the employee where no agreement has been signed. In Italy, the individual contract sits on top of the CCNL, never beside it.

## Practical steps

1. **Map the role before the salary.** Sector, CCNL and level first; then the number.
2. **Read the agreement, not a summary from another country.** Swedish practice is a good instinct, not a guide to the Italian text.
3. **Budget the full cost.** Include 13th month, any 14th, extra leave, sector funds and employer contributions.
4. **Name the CCNL and the level in the offer and the contract.**
5. **Recheck on promotion.** A new level can mean new minimums.

## How an EOR handles it

With an Employer of Record (EOR), we are the legal employer in Italy. We choose the CCNL and the level, explain the choice in the quote, apply the pay tables and update them when the agreement is renewed. You keep the day-to-day management.

For a side-by-side view of Swedish and Italian rules, see [Italy vs Sweden](/italy-vs-sweden.html). To see what a role costs under the right agreement, use the [cost calculator](/calculator.html).

Every Nordic manager knows the summer pattern. Somewhere around Midsummer, the office starts emptying, and for weeks little moves. Italy has the same phenomenon, but it peaks later. Many Italian companies, suppliers and customers slow right down in August, around Ferragosto on 15 August.

For a Nordic company with people in Italy, this offset is an opportunity, if you plan it. Unplanned, it becomes two summers of poor coverage.

## The Italian calendar

Italy has twelve national public holidays plus a local patron saint's day, which differs by city: Milan, Rome, Turin, Bologna and Naples each have their own. Public holidays are paid and do not count against holiday.

Annual holiday is at least four weeks by law, part of it to be taken in the year it accrues. Most CCNLs add paid hours off. In many sectors employees take a long block in August, and some factories close for part of the month.

## Where the calendars collide

- **Nordic July.** Your Italian team is working, but their Nordic colleagues, approvers and support functions are on holiday.
- **Italian August.** Your Nordic team is back, but Italian customers, suppliers and colleagues are away.
- **Public holidays.** Neither side's holidays exist in the other's calendar: Midsummer and National Day at home; Liberation Day, Republic Day and the patron saint's day in Italy.

## Turning the offset into coverage

**Plan both summers at once.** Agree holiday plans in spring for both teams. A simple rule works: someone with authority is always reachable for the Italian team in July, and someone covers Italian accounts in August.

**Use the Italian team in July.** Support, customer success, QA and operations roles in Italy can keep services running while the Nordic office is quiet, and the reverse in August.

**Align Italian holiday with Italian customers.** A seller or field engineer serving Italian accounts should usually take their main holiday in August. Insisting on July because "that is when we close" helps nobody.

**Mind approvals and payroll.** Payroll inputs, expense approvals and contract signatures still need someone in July. Name a deputy.

## A shared calendar

Keep one calendar that shows:

- Nordic and Italian public holidays;
- the patron saint's day for each Italian employee's city;
- planned holiday blocks for both teams;
- release dates, trade fairs and customer events.

It prevents the most common avoidable mistakes: a launch on an Italian holiday, a review meeting in Ferragosto week, or a July invoice approval nobody is there to give.

## Records and liability

Holiday is a right, and the employer has a say on timing within the rules. Track accrued and taken days and hours off for each employee. Unused leave grows as a liability and is paid at exit. In our monthly summary you see the balances, so you can push for leave to be taken before it accumulates.

## Bridges

Italians make use of *ponti*, bridges: when a public holiday falls on a Tuesday or Thursday, many take the Monday or Friday off with an hour-off or holiday day. Expect lower availability around those dates and plan them in the calendar.

As Employer of Record (EOR), we apply the CCNL entitlements and keep the balances. You plan the work.

## Questions we hear from Nordic companies

**Can we require Italian staff to take holiday in July like the Nordic office?**
The employer has a say on timing within the law and the CCNL, but a rule that ignores the Italian market rarely works. Customer-facing staff are usually more useful in July and better off on holiday in August. Agree it in spring and document it.

**Do Italian employees work on Nordic public holidays?**
Yes. They follow Italian public holidays. A Nordic holiday is a normal working day in Italy, and the reverse. This is often an advantage: someone is always available.

**What about company shutdown weeks?**
If your company closes for a period, include the Italian team in the plan early and check how the CCNL treats collective holiday. We reflect it in payroll and in the leave balances.

For statutory leave in detail, read [25 days at home, four weeks in Italy](/articles/holiday-25-days-vs-italian-statutory-leave.html). For the legal comparison, see [Italy vs Sweden](/italy-vs-sweden.html).

A US company hiring in Italy has to unlearn at-will employment. A Swedish company does not. Under the Employment Protection Act (LAS) you already need objective grounds to dismiss, and you already work with notice periods that grow with service. Italy is built on the same principle: employment is stable, and the employer has to justify ending it.

That is the good news. The detail still differs, and the detail is where cases are lost. This article is an orientation, not legal advice on a specific exit.

## The Swedish baseline

Under LAS, termination must be in writing and rest on objective grounds: shortage of work or reasons relating to the employee. In redundancies, selection normally follows seniority, and an employer may exempt up to three employees whose skills are especially important. Employer notice is at least one month, rising to two months after two years and up to six months after ten years; the employee gives at least one month ([Øresunddirekt](https://oresunddirekt.dk/en/working-in-sweden/when-you-stop-working/termination-of-employment-in-sweden/)).

Norwegian readers will recognise the same structure: dismissal must be objectively justified, notice is one month under five years of service and grows after that ([Altinn](https://cms12.info.altinn.no/en/start-and-run-business/working-conditions/print-termination-of-employment-relationships/redundancy)). Danish readers start from a more flexible position, with the Salaried Employees Act notice of one to six months ([Business in Denmark](https://businessindenmark.virk.dk/guidance/employment-and-dismissal/resignation-and-termination/)); they will find Italy the biggest change.

## The Italian grounds

Italian law recognises three broad grounds for dismissal by the employer:

- **Just cause.** Conduct so serious that the relationship cannot continue even for the notice period. Close to the Swedish summary dismissal for serious breach.
- **Justified subjective reason.** A significant breach of duties that is less serious than just cause. Notice applies.
- **Justified objective reason.** Reasons linked to the organisation, such as a role that no longer exists. The employer may need to show that the person could not be placed in another position.

Some situations have their own rules, such as absence for illness beyond the protected period set by the CCNL.

Certain dismissals are not just costly but void: those linked to discrimination, to pregnancy or parental leave, or to the employee exercising a legal right. Swedish managers will find this intuitive.

## Procedure weighs more than in Sweden

In Sweden, a dismissal with weak grounds is the main risk. In Italy, a dismissal with good grounds and the wrong procedure is a risk of its own.

- **Disciplinary dismissals** need a written charge, a period for the employee to respond, and only then a decision. Skipping a step can sink the case.
- **The letter** must be in writing and state the reason where the law requires it. Vague or late letters are a frequent cause of lost disputes.
- **Consequences** of an unjustified dismissal are compensation and, in some cases, reinstatement.

There is no Italian equivalent of the Swedish seniority order (turordning) as you know it from LAS. Collective redundancies have their own procedure and selection criteria, which an EOR or a lawyer should run.

## Notice comes from the CCNL

LAS sets notice by statute. In Italy, notice usually comes from the national collective agreement (CCNL) that applies to the role, by level and seniority. It can be a few weeks for junior roles and several months for senior ones. If the employer wants the person to stop working at once, it can usually pay in lieu of notice. If the employee leaves without serving notice, the employer can generally claim an indemnity.

## Resignation is formal too

An Italian employee resigns through an official online procedure, not by email. This protects both sides: the company has a clear record that the decision was the employee's own.

## Agreed exits

As in Sweden, many exits end in a settlement. In Italy the agreement often needs to be signed in a protected setting, such as before a labour office or union representative, to be final. A private document alone may not stop a later claim.

## What the employee receives at the end

Here Italy adds lines that do not exist under LAS:

- unused holiday and hours off;
- the accrued share of the 13th month and any 14th;
- the TFR, the end-of-service accrual of 6.91% of pay a year, unless it has been paid monthly into a pension fund;
- notice pay where it applies.

The TFR is the item Nordic finance teams most often miss. In our EOR set-up it goes monthly into the fund the employee chooses, so no liability builds up.

## Practical habits

1. Use the probation period actively. It is the one window where either side can leave freely.
2. Keep written records of performance discussions and warnings, as you would before a Swedish personal-reasons dismissal.
3. Never announce a dismissal verbally first.
4. Speak to the employer of record or counsel before you start, not after.
5. Plan the final payslip and the return of equipment and access together.

For the full comparison table, see [Italy vs Sweden](/italy-vs-sweden.html). For how notice and accruals affect cost, try the [cost calculator](/calculator.html).

content: The Nordic region has a strong life sciences sector: large pharma groups, biotech clusters around Copenhagen, Lund and Stockholm, and a growing medtech scene in Finland. Italy is one of Europe's largest pharmaceutical producers and runs a large number of clinical trials. For a Nordic company running a trial or preparing a launch, Italian sites, doctors and patients often matter. That usually means people on the ground before there is an Italian company. ## The first roles Nordic biotech and medtech companies typically start with: - **Clinical research associates (CRAs)** to monitor Italian trial sites; - **clinical trial managers** for country-level coordination; - **regulatory affairs specialists** for submissions and contact with the Italian medicines agency (AIFA) and ethics committees; - **pharmacovigilance** staff; - **medical science liaisons** to work with key opinion leaders; - later, **market access** and **medical sales** roles. Many CRAs are home-based and travel to sites, which suits a company without an office. ## Where the talent is - **Milan and Lombardy**: the largest concentration of pharma companies, CROs and hospitals. - **Rome and Lazio**, including the Latina area with its pharmaceutical production. - **Tuscany**: Siena and Florence, with vaccines and life sciences research. - **Naples**: universities, hospitals and pharma. Italian life sciences graduates are well trained, and many have worked for CROs or multinational sponsors, so they know international SOPs. ## The contract Most roles fall under the Chemical-Pharmaceutical agreement (CCNL Chimico-farmaceutico). It includes a supplementary pension fund and a health fund with employer contributions, which belong in the budget. Commercial roles in distribution companies may fall under Commerce and services. ## Compliance points - **Regulated roles.** Some positions, such as the local pharmacovigilance contact or the scientific information manager, may need registration with AIFA, and some may require a local entity. Check before you hire for these. [confirm which roles require a local entity or registration] - **Medical representatives.** Scientific information to doctors follows Italian rules on qualifications and reporting; hire people who already meet them. - **Confidentiality.** Contracts cover trial data, patient data and inventions, aligned with GDPR, which Nordic companies already apply. - **Car and territory.** Field roles usually have a company car and a defined territory. ## Timing A typical pattern: one or two CRAs and a clinical trial manager during the trial, regulatory and medical affairs as approval approaches, then a local company at launch. An Employer of Record (EOR) covers the first two phases. When you register products or open an office, we transfer staff to your company without a break in service. ## Non-EU staff Some candidates, and some staff you may want to move from Copenhagen or Stockholm, are not EU citizens. They need an Italian work permit; we handle it as the employer, for €2,500 per case. ## Cost A home-based CRA costs the gross salary, employer contributions, 13th month, TFR, CCNL funds and travel on actuals, plus €250 a month. The [cost calculator](/calculator.html) gives the base. ## Questions we hear from Nordic companies **Can a CRA employed through an EOR monitor sites for our trial?** Yes. The CRA works under your SOPs and your clinical operations team. We are the employer; the scientific and regulatory responsibility remains with the sponsor or CRO as defined in your trial set-up. **Do life sciences roles have special working-time rules?** Site travel and irregular hours are common. The CCNL rules on working time and travel apply; define the expected travel pattern before the offer so that it can be priced. **What about non-compete clauses for MSLs?** They are possible under the Italian conditions: written, paid, and limited in time, place and activity. For many roles confidentiality and IP clauses are enough. ## In short Italy is a natural place for Nordic life sciences companies to run trials and prepare launches. Start with CRAs and clinical managers through an EOR, add regulatory and medical affairs as approval approaches, and check early which roles need registration or a local entity. Budget for the Chemical-Pharmaceutical CCNL funds and travel. When you launch, move the team into your own company without a break in service. See [Life sciences in Italy](/hire-pharma-life-sciences-italy.html) for roles and clusters, and [work permits](/visas.html) for non-EU hires.

Nordic employers know the value of tax-efficient benefits: lunch cards, wellness allowances, a company phone. Italy has its own set, and two of them are worth knowing before you make an offer: meal vouchers and fringe benefits.

## Meal vouchers (buoni pasto)

Meal vouchers are the most common Italian benefit. The employee receives a voucher for each working day, usually loaded on a card, to spend in restaurants, bars and supermarkets.

The point is tax. In 2026, meal vouchers are exempt from income tax and social contributions up to:

- **€10 a day** for electronic vouchers;
- **€4 a day** for paper vouchers.

Above those amounts, the excess is taxed as salary. In practice almost everyone uses electronic vouchers.

For a remote employee with no company canteen, meal vouchers are an efficient way to raise net pay without the cost of an equivalent gross raise. Italian candidates notice them and often ask.

A few practical points:

- vouchers are normally given for days actually worked, not for holiday or sick days;
- the CCNL or a company policy sets who receives them;
- part-time employees receive them according to the policy, usually on days worked.

## Fringe benefits

Italy also has a yearly tax-free threshold for other benefits in kind, such as gift cards, shopping vouchers and payment of utility bills. In 2026 it is:

- **€1,000 a year** for employees in general;
- **€2,000 a year** for employees with dependent children.

The threshold is a cliff. If the total value exceeds it, the whole amount becomes taxable, not just the excess. Track it.

## Other benefits

- **Supplementary health cover.** Contributions to health funds, often set by the CCNL, are exempt up to €3,615.20 a year.
- **Supplementary pension.** The TFR and extra contributions can go to a pension fund; the nearest thing to a Nordic occupational pension top-up.
- **Company car.** For business and private use, taxed on a flat share of a standard cost that depends on emissions.
- **Laptop and phone.** Work tools, documented as such, are not taxable salary.

## What does not translate

Some Nordic benefits have no direct Italian equivalent, and their tax treatment in Italy may differ. Before you copy a group benefits policy, ask us which items work in Italy and which become taxable salary.

## Building a package

A simple, competitive package for an Italian professional might include:

1. electronic meal vouchers for each working day;
2. the CCNL health fund, or a better plan;
3. TFR into a pension fund of the employee's choice;
4. laptop and phone;
5. a written lavoro agile agreement.

Each item is easy to explain in an offer and easy to run through payroll.

## Cost

Meal vouchers and benefits within the thresholds cost you their face value, without employer contributions on top. That makes them cheaper per euro of net pay than salary. We show them as separate lines in the quote and the monthly invoice.

## Questions we hear from Nordic companies

**Can we give meal vouchers to a remote employee?**
Yes, under a company policy. They are a common way to support remote staff who have no canteen.

**Do benefits count for the TFR?**
Benefits within the tax-free thresholds are generally not salary, so they do not raise the TFR or contributions. Salary items do.

**Can we change the benefit package later?**
Benefits granted by contract or established practice can be hard to withdraw. Start with what you are sure you will keep, and add later.

**Do meal vouchers appear on the payslip?**
Yes, as a non-taxable line within the daily limit. Any excess above the limit is shown and taxed as salary. The employee sees exactly what they received each month, and you see the cost in the payroll summary.

## In short

Electronic meal vouchers up to €10 a day and fringe benefits within the yearly threshold are the simplest way to raise an Italian employee's net pay at a lower cost than salary. Track the fringe-benefit threshold carefully, because exceeding it makes the whole amount taxable. Before copying a Nordic benefit package, check each item: some translate directly, others become ordinary taxable salary in Italy.

See the full list of pay and benefit items in [From RAL to net pay](/italy-salary-components.html). Model a package in the [cost calculator](/calculator.html).

You have found the right person in Milan or Bologna. The interviews went well. Now you need an offer that the candidate signs, against local employers and other foreign companies. Nordic companies have real advantages here: reputation, work-life balance, flat structure. They also make the same few mistakes.

## Start from the Italian market

Price the role against the Italian market in the city where the person lives, not as a discount on a Stockholm or Oslo salary. A number that looks generous after currency conversion may still be below what a strong Italian candidate expects, and the reverse is possible too.

Ask the candidate for their current RAL and the number of instalments. Italians are used to that question.

## State the offer the Italian way

- **RAL**: gross annual pay.
- **Instalments**: 13 or 14, or 12 if the 13th and 14th are spread.
- **CCNL and level.** A named agreement and level reassure the candidate that the job is properly framed.
- **Contract type**: permanent, with probation length.
- **Variable pay** with a written plan.
- **Benefits**: meal vouchers, health fund, pension fund for the TFR, laptop and phone.
- **Place of work and remote terms.**

Vague offers lose to precise ones.

## Show the net

Italian candidates think in net monthly pay. Between RAL and net are the employee's social contributions (9.19%), income tax (IRPEF at 23% up to €28,000, 33% to €50,000 and 43% above, reduced by employment credits), and the regional and municipal surcharges for their city.

Give a net estimate with the offer. The [net pay calculator](/net-pay-calculator.html) covers the five main cities. Showing you have done the work is itself persuasive.

## Answer the stability question

A strong Italian candidate leaving a local employer will ask: who is my employer, and is this a real Italian contract? With an Employer of Record (EOR), the answer is clear. We are the legal employer in Italy, the contract is a normal Italian employment contract under a CCNL, contributions go to INPS, and the TFR builds up as for any employee. Our [page for employees](/employees.html) explains it in plain words; send it with the offer.

## Use your Nordic strengths

- **Work-life balance.** Clear working hours, real disconnection, respect for holiday. Many Italian professionals are looking for exactly that.
- **Trust and autonomy.** Flat structures and less micromanagement.
- **Remote work done properly.** A written lavoro agile agreement, equipment, and a manager who measures output.
- **Parental leave culture.** Fathers encouraged to use their optional leave.

Say these things concretely in the conversation. They are often worth more than a small salary difference.

## Avoid these mistakes

- **Offering a fixed term "to start with".** It signals risk.
- **Monthly salary without explanation.** The candidate will multiply by twelve, or by fourteen, and one of you will be disappointed.
- **Bonus without a plan.** "Up to" means nothing to an Italian candidate without written rules.
- **Equity as a substitute for salary.** Options are appreciated but rarely decisive, and their Italian tax treatment needs explaining.
- **Slow paperwork.** A week between verbal yes and written offer is long enough to lose a candidate.

## Timing

With an EOR, we can turn an agreed offer into an Italian contract within days for EU and EEA citizens. Agree the start date with the candidate's notice period in mind: Italian notice periods come from their current CCNL and can be several weeks or months.

## Checklist

1. Market-based RAL and instalments.
2. CCNL and level.
3. Permanent contract and probation.
4. Written variable plan.
5. Benefits listed.
6. Net estimate attached.
7. Remote terms.
8. Start date matched to notice.

## Questions we hear from Nordic companies

**Should we negotiate in gross or net?**
State the offer in RAL, but always show the net estimate. Candidates decide on net.

**How long do Italian candidates take to decide?**
Usually not long, if the offer is clear. Delays usually come from missing information: contract type, CCNL, benefits or remote terms. Send everything at once.

## In short

Price the role against the Italian market, state the offer in RAL with instalments, name the CCNL and level, show the net, and send everything at once. Lead with what Nordic employers do well: balance, trust, real remote work. Answer the stability question with a clear explanation of the EOR. Do these things quickly and most good candidates will sign.

Price the offer in the [cost calculator](/calculator.html) before you send it.

content: A Swedish, Danish or Finnish citizen can move to Italy and start work without a permit, as can Norwegians and Icelanders under EEA rules. But many Nordic tech and engineering teams are international. The developer from India in your Stockholm office, the engineer from Brazil in Copenhagen or the product manager from the US in Helsinki may hold a Nordic residence and work permit. That permit does not give them the right to work in Italy. If one of them wants to move to Italy, or you want to place them there, they need an Italian work permit first. ## Two main routes ### EU Blue Card For highly qualified roles above a minimum salary threshold. In 2026 the threshold is about €36,300 gross a year; the official reference still needs confirming. The Blue Card is not subject to the annual quotas and gives mobility rights within the EU. If the employee already holds a Blue Card from Sweden, Finland or another member state, intra-EU mobility rules can simplify the process. The details depend on the case. [confirm intra-EU Blue Card mobility procedure for Italy] ### Ordinary work permit under the quotas Other employees come in under the annual quota system, the Decreto Flussi. The 2026–2028 planning sets, for 2026, 43,300 non-seasonal entries: 25,000 for nationals of certain countries, 18,000 for countries with agreements, and 300 for stateless people and refugees (investireoggi.it, secondary source). Applications are filed in set windows, so timing depends on the calendar. For most professional roles at Nordic salary levels, the Blue Card is the route to try first. ## The steps 1. **Eligibility.** We check degree, salary and role against the route. 2. **Italian employment contract.** As Employer of Record (EOR), we are the Italian employer and sign the contract under the right CCNL, conditional on the permit. 3. **Work authorisation (nulla osta).** We file it with the Immigration Office (Sportello Unico). 4. **Visa.** The employee applies at the Italian consulate responsible for where they live, which may be in the Nordics. 5. **Arrival.** Residence permit application, tax code, registration with the national health service. 6. **First payslip.** ## Planning around it - **Do not resign the Nordic job too early.** The employee should keep their current permit and job until the Italian visa is granted. - **Family.** Family members usually follow through family reunification, with its own procedure. - **Pension and social security.** Contributions paid in the Nordics stay there; Italian contributions start with the Italian employment. EU coordination rules help combine periods for some benefits. - **Housing and relocation.** Tax code, housing, bank account and health service registration take time; our relocation support covers them. ## Cost The permit case costs €2,500, covering the eligibility check, nulla osta application, consulate appointment and residence permit. The employment cost and our €250 monthly fee start with the employment. ## Questions we hear from Nordic companies **Can the employee keep working for us remotely from Italy while waiting?** Not without the right to work in Italy. Working in Italy before the permit is granted is a risk for both sides. Keep them in their current role until the visa is issued. **Does the Nordic employer have to end the contract?** Usually the Nordic employment ends when the Italian employment starts. Coordinate end and start dates so there is no gap in pay or insurance. **Can a spouse work in Italy?** Family members who join through family reunification can usually work. The conditions depend on the permit; we check them as part of the case. **How long does it take?** Blue Card cases are generally faster than quota permits, which depend on application windows. We give a timeline after the eligibility check. ## In short A Nordic residence permit does not allow work in Italy. For a non-EU employee who moves, start with the Blue Card if the role and salary qualify, and with the quota route otherwise. Sign the Italian contract conditionally, file the nulla osta, and let the employee keep the Nordic job until the visa is granted. Plan housing, family and the first payslip as one project, and leave enough time for each step. See [work permits](/visas.html) for an overview, and estimate the salary cost in the [cost calculator](/calculator.html).

Nordic employment contracts often carry a standard restraint clause: a non-compete for senior staff, a non-solicitation of customers and colleagues, and confidentiality. In each Nordic country the clause is tested for reasonableness under local rules, and in some cases the employer must pay compensation during the restricted period.

Bring that clause to Italy unchanged and it will probably fail. Italian law does not just ask whether a restriction is reasonable. It lists conditions that must all be met. Miss one and the clause is void.

## The Italian conditions

### 1. Written form

The non-compete must be in writing: in the employment contract or a separate signed agreement. A handbook line or a verbal promise does not count.

### 2. A defined activity

The restriction must relate to what the employee actually does for you. It cannot prevent the person from working in their profession at all. "Any role in the industry" is likely void. Tie it to the products, services or functions where the employee holds sensitive knowledge.

### 3. A defined territory

State the area, and keep it reasonable. A worldwide ban for a mid-level seller who covered northern Italy invites a challenge. Match it to where you actually compete and where the employee had exposure.

### 4. A time limit set by law

The maximum is 3 years after the end of employment, 5 years for executives. If a clause runs longer, the duration is cut to the legal maximum. That is the only point where Italian law saves part of a clause.

### 5. A real payment

This is where Nordic templates usually fail. The employee must receive a specific payment for accepting the restriction, separate from salary, and proportionate to what they give up. A token sum is treated as no payment. A wider and longer restriction needs higher pay; there is no formula, and courts decide case by case.

The payment can be made during employment or after it ends, but it must be identifiable as the price of the non-compete. If it disappears into a general raise, expect a dispute.

## Loyalty during employment

While employed, the employee already owes a duty of loyalty: no work for a competitor, no use of company information against you. You do not need a non-compete for that period. The clause only matters after the job ends.

## Common mistakes

- **Copying the Nordic or group template.** A choice of Swedish or Danish law does not override Italian mandatory rules for someone working in Italy.
- **No separate payment.** Employment itself is not consideration.
- **Overbroad scope.** Industry-wide or worldwide bans.
- **Adding it later.** Agree it at hiring, with proper pay.
- **Assuming non-solicits are safe.** A broad ban on contacting customers can be treated as a non-compete and tested against the same rules.

## Do you need one?

For many roles, confidentiality, IP assignment and the duty of loyalty are enough. Use a non-compete where the person has genuinely sensitive customer or technical knowledge, and accept that it has a price.

## Steps

1. Decide whether you need the restriction at all.
2. Define activity, territory and duration narrowly, in writing.
3. Set a payment you can defend, and label it.
4. Have the final text reviewed under Italian law before signature.
5. Put the payment in the budget.

With an Employer of Record (EOR), the clause is signed between the employee and us as legal employer, protecting your business interest. We include its cost in the quote.

## Questions we hear from Nordic companies

**How much should the payment be?**
There is no formula. It must be proportionate to the restriction: wider scope, longer time and a larger territory need more. Ask us for the range used in similar roles before you fix the amount.

**Can we release the employee from the non-compete when they leave?**
Only if the clause and Italian rules allow it, and the conditions matter. An option to withdraw at will can make the clause void. Draft it carefully at the start.

## In short

An Italian non-compete must be written, paid, limited in time, territory and activity, and proportionate. A Nordic template rarely meets all five conditions. Decide whether you need it, draft it narrowly at hiring, price it honestly and budget the payment.

See the non-compete row in [Italy vs Sweden](/italy-vs-sweden.html), and model the payment in the [cost calculator](/calculator.html).

A Swedish finance team thinks of pension in two layers. Employer contributions to the state, 31.42% of gross pay in 2026 in total ([Skatteverket](https://www.skatteverket.se/servicelankar/otherlanguages/englishengelska/businessesandemployers.4.2fb39afe18dabf1e4d24a3d.html)), and an occupational pension that usually comes from the collective agreement ([Medlingsinstitutet](https://www.mi.se/app/uploads/the-swedish-model-and-collective-agreements.pdf)). Norway and Denmark have their own versions of the same idea.

Italy also has two layers, but they are built differently. Knowing where each euro goes makes the Italian cost line easier to defend in a budget meeting.

## Layer one: the state pension through INPS

The main Italian pension contribution is called IVS: invalidity, old age and survivors. It is paid to INPS, the national social security institute, on the employee's taxable pay.

- The **employer share** is **23.81%**.
- The **employee share** is **9.19%**, withheld from gross pay.

Together that is a 33% pension contribution on taxable pay, and the employer carries most of it. It does not appear on the payslip as a deduction from the employee, so managers sometimes forget it exists. Finance should not.

IVS is not the only employer contribution. Unemployment, sickness and maternity, family allowances and guarantee funds bring the employer total to roughly 30% depending on sector and size, plus INAIL injury insurance. The Swedish total and the Italian total land in the same range. The Norwegian total, at 14.1% in zone I, is much lower, so Norwegian budgets need the biggest adjustment.

The IVS figures come from a professional source, not from INPS directly. For a signed offer we confirm the rate for the specific role.

## Two numbers to know for senior hires

For employees first insured from 1996 onwards, pension contributions stop above a yearly earnings ceiling of €122,295 in 2026. And the employee rate goes up by one point on pay above €56,224 a year. Both matter when you hire a senior engineer or a country manager.

## Layer two: the TFR

The second layer has no exact Nordic equivalent. The TFR (trattamento di fine rapporto) is an accrual of 6.91% of gross pay a year, owed to the employee when employment ends for any reason (Civil Code art. 2120).

By default it is a liability that sits with the employer and grows every year. The employee can instead direct it to a supplementary pension fund. Then it behaves much like an occupational pension contribution: paid every month, invested for the employee, gone from your balance sheet.

In our EOR set-up we pay the TFR monthly into the fund the employee chooses. That is the closest Italian match to what a Swedish employer does with occupational pension, and it keeps your cost flat.

## Supplementary funds through the CCNL

Some CCNLs, such as the Chemical-Pharmaceutical agreement, add a sector pension fund with an employer contribution. If the employee joins, that contribution is part of the employment cost. It is the Italian counterpart to an agreement-based pension, but smaller and optional for the employee.

## Retirement age

The standard Italian old-age pension starts at 67 with at least 20 years of contributions. Early retirement is possible at any age after 42 years and 10 months of contributions for men, one year less for women. From 2027 the requirements rise by one month, and by three months from 2028.

## Building the budget line

1. Start with the gross salary (RAL).
2. Add the employer pension share of 23.81% of taxable pay.
3. Add the other employer contributions and INAIL as separate lines.
4. Add the TFR at 6.91%.
5. Add any CCNL pension or health fund contribution.
6. Compare with the budget approved for the role.

If the approved budget was built on the Swedish model, steps 2 and 3 will be close. Step 4 is the new line. If it was built on the Norwegian model, the whole contribution layer will be higher.

## Questions we hear from Nordic companies

**Can we add a Nordic-style occupational pension?**
Yes, through contributions to an Italian supplementary pension fund on top of the TFR. Employer contributions to such funds have tax advantages within limits. We set it up as part of the contract.

**Can an Italian employee join our Nordic pension plan?**
Usually not in a simple way. Italian rules and tax treatment apply to someone employed and insured in Italy. Use an Italian fund instead.

**Is the TFR safe if the employer has problems?**
There is a TFR guarantee fund within INPS. If the TFR is paid monthly into a pension fund, it is already outside the employer.

Run the numbers for a real salary in the [cost calculator](/calculator.html), and compare the systems in [Italy vs Sweden](/italy-vs-sweden.html).

Nordic managers are better prepared for parental leave than almost anyone. In Sweden each child brings 480 days of parental benefit, 390 of them at sickness-benefit level, with 90 days reserved for each parent ([Försäkringskassan](https://forsakringskassan.se/english/parents/when-the-child-is-born/parental-benefit)). Fathers taking months off is normal. Teams plan around it as a matter of routine.

Italy protects parenthood strongly too, but the shape is different. If you plan an Italian absence with Swedish expectations, the dates and the cost will not match.

## The Italian structure

- **Maternity leave** is compulsory: 5 months around the birth, paid mainly through INPS. The employee cannot waive it and the employer cannot ask her to.
- **Paternity leave** is 10 working days, paid, to be taken around the birth.
- **Optional parental leave** comes on top for both parents over the following years, partly paid.

Two consequences follow. First, the mother's absence is predictable and fixed. Second, fathers in Italy take much shorter leave by default than Nordic fathers do. Some Italian fathers will be pleased to work for a Nordic company that encourages them to use their optional leave. Say so, and mean it.

Confirm the exact entitlements for the employee's contract and CCNL before setting dates. Some CCNLs top up what INPS pays.

## Protection from dismissal

As in the Nordics, an employee is protected against dismissal linked to pregnancy and parental leave. In Italy the protected period is defined by law and dismissals in that period are generally void. Do not plan a reorganisation that touches the role while the person is away. The job is being covered, not filled by someone else.

## The first conversation

Let the employee lead. Ask about the expected timeline and how much contact they want during leave. Write the answer down. Keep it practical: thank them, explain that you will plan coverage, ask who handles their key tasks today, and agree a date to review the plan.

Do not ask about plans for more children or about returning. That is as unacceptable in Italy as at home.

## Plan the work, not the person

List what the employee does in a normal month and sort each task:

- **Pause:** can wait for their return.
- **Share:** colleagues can absorb small pieces.
- **Cover:** needs a dedicated person.

The "cover" list is usually shorter than feared.

## Covering the role

- **Redistribute internally** for short gaps. Adjust the goals of whoever takes on more.
- **Hire a fixed-term replacement.** Italian law allows a fixed-term contract to replace an employee on leave; the purpose must be clear in writing. A replacement needs a few weeks to become useful, so start early.
- **Use a contractor for defined deliverables**, not for the same daily work, which risks reclassification.

Through an Employer of Record (EOR), we draft the replacement contract under the same CCNL.

## Budget for the overlap

The employer's cost for the absent employee does not always drop to zero. INPS pays most of the maternity allowance, but the employer may owe a top-up under the CCNL, and items such as the 13th month and holiday keep accruing in some situations. At the same time you pay the replacement. Ask us for a breakdown before the leave starts: what INPS pays, what you pay, what the CCNL adds, what the replacement costs.

## Handover and return

A handover is a document: recurring tasks, where files live, key contacts, open projects, decisions that need an owner. Walk through it with whoever takes over, well before the planned start, because babies do not follow plans.

For the return, agree a short catch-up before day one, a lighter first week and a check-in after a month. Italian parents have certain rights to adjusted arrangements after leave. Treat those requests as normal planning.

## Common mistakes

- Planning late.
- Getting in touch during the leave without having agreed it.
- Treating the replacement as permanent.
- Forgetting the cost until the first payroll.
- Assuming Nordic leave patterns apply.

## Questions we hear from Nordic companies

**Can an Italian father take long leave as in Sweden?**
He can use optional parental leave on top of the paternity leave, but it is partly paid. A Nordic company can encourage it and, if it wishes, top up pay as a company benefit. We can run that through payroll.

See the leave rows in [Italy vs Sweden](/italy-vs-sweden.html), and model the cost of cover in the [cost calculator](/calculator.html).
