content: Nordic companies often pay a yearly bonus on company or team results. In Sweden or Denmark it is simply taxed as salary. In Italy, a bonus can be taxed very differently depending on how it is set up. A qualifying productivity bonus, *premio di risultato*, is taxed at a flat **1%** in 2026, on up to **€5,000** a year per employee, instead of normal income tax rates that run up to 43%. That difference is large enough to shape how you design variable pay for your Italian team. ## What qualifies The reduced rate is meant for bonuses linked to measurable improvements in productivity, profitability, quality, efficiency or innovation. In broad terms: - the bonus must be based on a company or territorial agreement that defines the targets and how they are measured; - the targets must be objective and verifiable, with a measurement period; - the payment must depend on reaching an improvement, not just on the passage of time; - the employee must be within the income limit set by law. The limit applied in 2025 was €80,000 of employment income; confirmation for 2026 was not found in our source. A bonus paid at the manager's discretion, or a guaranteed bonus, does not qualify. ## Ordinary bonus vs productivity bonus | | Ordinary bonus | Qualifying productivity bonus | |---|---|---| | Income tax | IRPEF at the marginal rate (23%, 33% or 43%) plus surcharges | 1% flat, up to €5,000 a year | | Basis | Any policy, even discretionary | A written agreement with measurable targets | | Eligibility | Every employee | Within the income limit | | Employer contributions | Normal | Normal [confirm any contribution relief] | For an employee in the 33% band, a €5,000 ordinary bonus loses about a third to income tax; the same amount as a qualifying productivity bonus loses €50. ## The welfare option Under the same rules, the employee can often choose to receive part or all of the productivity bonus as welfare benefits instead of cash: health, education, care services and similar. These can receive even more favourable treatment [confirm 2026 welfare conversion rules]. It is worth offering, because some employees value it. ## What this means for a Nordic company **Design team or company targets, not only individual ones.** The Italian rules reward measurable collective improvement. That fits Nordic management style well. **Put it in writing before the period starts.** A plan designed after the results are known will not qualify. **Keep individual bonuses separate.** Commissions for sellers and discretionary rewards remain ordinary pay. That is fine; just do not mix them into the productivity plan. **Mind the cap and the income limit.** Above €5,000, or above the income limit, normal taxation applies. ## Setting it up through an EOR With an Employer of Record (EOR), we are the employer in Italy, so the plan is set up under our company. We draft the plan on the targets you define, file what is required, and apply the 1% rate in payroll when the bonus is paid. You decide the targets and the amounts. ## Steps 1. Decide what you want to reward: revenue growth, delivery quality, cost reduction. 2. Define objective measures and the measurement period. 3. Set the bonus amounts, within €5,000 for the reduced rate. 4. Put the plan in writing before the period starts. 5. Measure, document and pay. ## Questions we hear from Nordic companies **Can one employee have a productivity plan?** The plan is a company-level instrument; it can cover a small team, but it must be based on the required agreement and measurable targets. We check whether your case fits. **Does a productivity bonus count for the TFR?** Treatment depends on how the bonus is structured. We show the effect in the quote. ## In short A well-designed productivity plan lets Italian employees keep almost all of a bonus up to €5,000 a year. It needs written, measurable targets set before the period starts, and it works best for team or company results, which suits Nordic management. Keep commissions and discretionary rewards separate as ordinary pay, and let us check eligibility and the income limit before the plan is announced. More on pay components in [From RAL to net pay](/italy-salary-components.html). To see the effect on cost, use the [cost calculator](/calculator.html).

Nordic managers like probation. It gives both sides time to see whether the hire works before the full employment protection applies. Sweden allows probationary employment of up to six months, and an employer that ends it must give at least two weeks' notice ([Business Sweden](https://www.business-sweden.com/497a82/contentassets/582cb98533254f61bce11da9af436cf8/2026/employing-staff---contracts-and-conditions-2026.pdf), [Øresunddirekt](https://oresunddirekt.dk/en/working-in-sweden/when-you-stop-working/termination-of-employment-in-sweden/)). Norway allows a trial period of up to six months as well.

Italy has the same tool, the *periodo di prova*. The maximum length is similar. The way it is set up, and the way it ends, are not.

## What it is

The Italian probation period is the first phase of an employment contract, usually an open-ended one. The employee is a full employee from day one: pay, contributions, holiday accrual, health and safety all apply. Probation is not a lighter category of worker, just as provanställning is not.

## The form rule

This is where Nordic companies slip. In Italy, probation exists only if it is written into the contract and signed before work starts. A clause that is missing, or signed after the first working day, is generally void. The employee then has full dismissal protection from the start.

The clause should also describe the tasks that are being tested. A clause that names no duties can be challenged, and if the job changes after hiring, the clause may not cover the new duties.

In Sweden the risk of a sloppy probation clause is that the job becomes permanent. In Italy the result is similar, but it happens more easily, because the formal requirements are stricter.

## How long

National law sets an outer limit, and the applicable collective agreement (CCNL) sets the working maximum for each level. Senior roles usually get longer periods than junior ones, up to about six months. The contract cannot go beyond what the CCNL allows, and the same title can carry a different maximum under a different agreement.

## Ending it

Here Italy is more flexible than Sweden. During the probation period either side can usually end the contract without notice, and the employer does not need to show the grounds required later. There is no two-week notice as in Sweden.

It is still not a free pass:

- the reason cannot be discriminatory or retaliatory;
- the trial must be real: if the person never had a fair chance to do the tasks named in the contract, a court may find the termination unjustified;
- protected situations such as pregnancy limit the employer's freedom;
- leaving someone without work and then ending the trial invites a dispute.

A clear, documented decision inside the window is low risk. The risk grows when the reason looks unrelated to performance.

## When probation ends

If nobody acts by the last day, the employment confirms automatically, and the time counts toward seniority. From then on the full Italian dismissal framework applies: a valid reason, a procedure and usually notice.

So the logic is the same as in Sweden. Flexibility sits at the start and then largely disappears. What differs is the margin for error: in Italy there is no notice period to soften a late decision, and silence is the decision.

## Practical steps

- Identify the CCNL and the maximum probation for the level before drafting.
- Put the clause in the contract and get it signed before day one.
- List the tasks the trial covers.
- Give real work and real feedback from the first week; Nordic one-to-ones fit well here.
- Hold a documented review well before the end date, not in the final days.
- Decide in time.

## With an employer of record

With an Employer of Record (EOR), the EOR is the legal employer and drafts the clause under the right CCNL. You run the work and the evaluation. In practice the decision is shared, so agree the review dates at the start. We put them in the onboarding plan.

## Questions we hear from Nordic companies

**Can we extend probation if we are unsure?**
Only within the CCNL maximum and, in general, not beyond it. Decide within the window. If you cannot decide, that is often a decision in itself.

**Does probation work for a fixed-term contract?**
Yes, proportionate to the contract length and within CCNL limits.

For the other differences between Swedish and Italian employment, read [Italy vs Sweden](/italy-vs-sweden.html). To price the hire, use the [cost calculator](/calculator.html).

In Sweden, salary talk is usually monthly. Italians speak almost exclusively in **RAL**: *retribuzione annua lorda*, gross annual pay.

If your hiring manager and your Italian candidate use different units, the negotiation goes wrong before it starts.

## What RAL includes

RAL is the total gross pay agreed for a year of work. It includes:

- the twelve monthly salaries;
- the 13th month, which every CCNL provides;
- the 14th month, where the CCNL provides it (for example Commerce and services);
- fixed allowances that are part of regular pay.

It does not include:

- variable pay, commissions and bonuses (unless guaranteed);
- meal vouchers and other benefits;
- employer contributions, INAIL and the TFR, which are employer costs on top.

## From RAL to a monthly payslip

Divide RAL by the number of instalments in the CCNL, 13 or 14, not by 12. If the 13th and 14th are spread over the year, as in our standard set-up, the monthly gross is RAL divided by 12. Same annual pay, different monthly line.

When a candidate says "my current RAL is X", ask how many instalments. When you make an offer, write both the RAL and the instalments.

## From RAL to net

Italian candidates compare offers on net monthly pay. Between RAL and net are the employee's social security contribution (9.19%, plus one point above €56,224 a year), IRPEF income tax at 23%, 33% and 43% by band, employment tax credits, and the regional and municipal surcharges of the city where they live.

The [net pay calculator](/net-pay-calculator.html) gives an estimate for Milan, Rome, Turin, Bologna and Naples. Show the candidate the number; it builds trust.

## From RAL to your cost

For your budget, RAL is the starting point, not the total. Add employer contributions of roughly 30%, INAIL, the TFR at 6.91% and any CCNL fund contributions. Then our €250 a month. The [cost calculator](/calculator.html) does this for two example CCNLs.

## Comparing with a Nordic salary

Do not convert a Swedish monthly salary at the exchange rate and multiply by twelve. Compare on two levels:

1. **Market level.** What does this role earn in the Italian city you are hiring in? Italian salaries are generally lower than Nordic ones, and the living costs differ too.
2. **Total cost.** What does the role cost you in Italy compared with at home, all employer items included?

A fair Italian offer is set against the Italian market, not as a discount on a Stockholm salary.

## Negotiation habits

- Italian candidates may expect some negotiation; the first number is not always the last.
- They value stability and clarity: a permanent contract, a named CCNL and level, and written benefits.
- They notice details: meal vouchers, the 14th month, remote-work terms, a laptop and phone.
- Be precise about variable pay. A percentage bonus without a written plan is worth little to them.

## The offer letter

State clearly:

- RAL and number of instalments;
- CCNL and level;
- variable pay and the plan that governs it;
- benefits;
- probation and notice;
- place of work and remote arrangement.

With an Employer of Record (EOR), we turn this into the Italian contract, so what the candidate signed matches what you promised.

## Questions we hear from Nordic companies

**Should we publish salary ranges in Italian job ads?**
It helps. Candidates respond better to ads with a RAL range, and it filters out mismatched expectations early. State whether the range is RAL and how many instalments.

**Is a raise also stated as RAL?**
Yes. Italians speak about raises in RAL too. Put any change into a written amendment, and check whether a new level under the CCNL applies.

**How do we compare two candidates in different cities?**
Same RAL, different net: local surcharges differ by city. Compare offers on RAL for fairness inside the team, and show each candidate the net for their own city so nobody is surprised by the first payslip.

## In short

Talk RAL with Italian candidates, always with the number of instalments. Show net monthly pay for their city, and budget on full employer cost. Do not convert a Nordic monthly salary into an Italian offer; price it against the Italian market.

More on offers in [How to make a job offer in Italy that closes](/articles/job-offer-italy-that-closes-nordic.html). For the components behind RAL, see [From RAL to net pay](/italy-salary-components.html).

Sooner or later your Italian employee will send you a screenshot of their payslip and ask a question. A Nordic manager used to a short lönespecifikation will see a dense page in Italian, with codes, accruals and three kinds of tax. Here is how to read it without becoming a payroll specialist.

## The header

The top block identifies employer and employee: our company as legal employer, the employee's tax code (codice fiscale), the CCNL, the level, the start date and seniority, and the pay period. If the CCNL or level looks wrong, raise it: it drives the minimum pay.

## Pay elements

The first table lists what the employee earned this month:

- **Minimo tabellare**: the CCNL minimum for the level.
- **Superminimo**: what you agreed above the minimum.
- **Scatti di anzianità**: seniority increments under the CCNL.
- **Overtime and allowances**: with the CCNL surcharges.
- **13th and 14th month**: as a lump sum in the months they are paid, or a pro-rata line every month if spread.
- **Variable pay**: commissions or bonuses for the period.

Together these make the gross pay for the month.

## Employee contributions

Next comes the employee's share of social security to INPS, around 9–10% of gross. The main part is the IVS pension contribution at 9.19%, with one extra point on pay above €56,224 a year.

These reduce taxable income.

## Income tax

Then **IRPEF**, the national income tax, calculated on taxable income at 23%, 33% and 43% by band and reduced by employment tax credits. Payroll works on a monthly estimate and adjusts during the year and in December.

Below IRPEF you will see the **regional** and **municipal surcharges**. They are typically withheld in instalments during the year following the one they relate to, so a new employee's first payslips may show none, or amounts relating to a previous employer. That surprises many people, including employees.

## Net pay

Gross minus contributions minus taxes, plus any non-taxable items such as expense reimbursements. This is the amount paid to the employee's account.

## The accrual block

Many payslips include a box showing balances: holiday days and hours off accrued and taken, and the TFR accrued. If the TFR goes monthly to a pension fund, the payslip shows the contribution to the fund.

## Employer cost is not on the payslip

The payslip shows the employee side. Employer contributions, INAIL and the TFR are not deductions from the employee, so most of them do not appear, or appear only as information. Your cost is in the payroll summary attached to our invoice.

## Typical questions and short answers

**"Why is my net different this month?"** Overtime, absences, a bonus, a tax adjustment or the start of local surcharges.

**"Why is December so high?"** The 13th month, if it is paid as a lump sum.

**"Why so much tax on my bonus?"** It is taxed at the marginal rate, unless it is a qualifying productivity bonus taxed at 1%.

**"What is this INPS line?"** The employee's pension and social security contribution.

When in doubt, the employee can ask us directly in Italian or English. Our payroll team answers the person who did the calculation.

## Questions we hear from Nordic companies

**Can the payslip be in English?**
The official payslip is in Italian. We provide an English explanation and the payroll summary in English, and our payroll team answers employees in English.

**Why does the first payslip of the year look different?**
Tax bands are applied fresh in January, and local surcharges for the previous year start to be withheld in instalments. Net pay can move even with no salary change.

**Who corrects a mistake?**
We do. If a payslip line is wrong, we correct it in the next payroll or with an adjustment, and explain the change to the employee and to you.

## In short

An Italian payslip has more lines than a Nordic one, but its logic is simple: earnings, employee contributions, income tax and surcharges, net pay, then balances. Your cost is in the payroll summary, not on the payslip. When an employee asks about a change, the answer is almost always overtime, an absence, a bonus, a tax adjustment or local surcharges, and our payroll team can explain the detail directly to them.

For the full structure, see [From RAL to net pay](/italy-salary-components.html). For an estimate of net pay by city, use the [net pay calculator](/net-pay-calculator.html).

Nordic tech companies compete for engineers in a small home market. Stockholm, Oslo, Copenhagen and Helsinki salaries are high, and good senior developers are hard to find. Italy offers a large, well-trained pool in the same time zone, with many engineers already used to working remotely for foreign companies.

## Where the developers are

- **Milan**: the largest tech market, with fintech, SaaS and consulting.
- **Turin**: strong engineering school, automotive and industrial software.
- **Rome**: large universities, public-sector and telecom software.
- **Bologna**: computer science, data and high-performance computing.
- **Pisa and Florence**: computer science tradition.
- **Naples**: a growing developer community around the Apple Developer Academy.

Many senior engineers have moved to smaller towns and work fully remote. Do not limit the search to the big cities.

## Channels

- **LinkedIn** works for most professional roles.
- **Italian job boards** and university career services reach junior and mid-level candidates.
- **Communities and meetups**, especially for languages and frameworks with active Italian groups.
- **Referrals** from your first Italian hire. Often the best channel once you have one.

Write the job ad in English for engineering roles; most Italian developers read it without difficulty. Add the essentials Italian candidates look for: contract type, RAL range, remote terms, and that they will be employed on an Italian contract.

## The process

Nordic hiring processes are usually lean and respectful, which Italian candidates appreciate. A few adjustments help:

- **Be fast.** Strong candidates get several offers. Two or three rounds, decided within two weeks, is a competitive advantage.
- **Explain the employment model early.** "You will be employed in Italy by our Employer of Record under a CCNL" answers the first question in every candidate's mind.
- **Give a salary range** in the first conversation.
- **Make the technical test proportionate.** Senior candidates drop out of long take-home assignments.
- **Introduce the team.** A call with future colleagues sells the culture better than any page.

## What makes them say yes

- A competitive RAL for the Italian market, stated with instalments.
- A permanent contract.
- Real remote work, with a written agreement and equipment.
- Meal vouchers and good benefits.
- Clear career levels and growth.
- English-speaking, international teams.
- Nordic work-life balance, which has a strong reputation.

Equity is appreciated, but rarely decisive on its own, and its Italian tax treatment needs explaining.

## After the hire

- **Onboarding in person** if you can: a week at the Nordic office in the first month.
- **Clear written priorities**: Italian engineers adapt quickly to flat structures, but appreciate explicit decisions.
- **Career path**: a visible level framework helps retention.

## The contract side

As Employer of Record (EOR), we employ the developer under the right CCNL, usually Commerce and services or Metalworking, with an IP assignment, confidentiality, and a lavoro agile agreement. On-call duties are paid under the CCNL. For EU citizens the start can be within days of signing.

## Questions we hear from Nordic companies

**Do we need to offer relocation to the Nordics?**
No. Most Italian developers who apply to Nordic scale-ups want to stay in Italy and work remotely. Offer travel for team weeks instead.

**How do we handle hardware and security?**
Ship a managed laptop or reimburse one, and write the rules into the lavoro agile agreement. Monitoring software must respect Italian limits on remote control.

**How fast can the first developer start?**
For an EU citizen, within days of a signed offer through an EOR, plus the notice period at the current employer, which comes from their CCNL. Ask about notice in the first interview, so that the start date you plan is realistic.

**Should the job ad be in Italian?**
For engineering roles English is usually fine and signals an international team. For customer-facing or support roles in Italian, write the ad in Italian.

## In short

Italy gives Nordic scale-ups a deep pool of developers in the same time zone. Search beyond the big cities, write clear ads with a RAL range and the employment model, run a fast process, and lead with what you do well: autonomy, balance and remote work done properly. After the hire, invest in in-person onboarding and a visible career path. The employment side, contract, IP, remote agreement and payroll, sits with us.

See [software engineers in Italy](/hire-software-engineers-italy.html), and estimate the cost in the [cost calculator](/calculator.html).

Many Nordic scale-ups are remote first. A new hire in Gothenburg or Tampere gets a laptop, access to the tools and a link to the remote-work policy. In Italy that is not enough. Remote work, called *lavoro agile* or smart working, is a formal arrangement that requires a written agreement between employer and employee.

## What lavoro agile is

Lavoro agile is a way of performing an ordinary employment relationship. Part of the work happens outside the company's premises, without a fixed workplace, organised by phases, cycles and goals rather than physical presence.

It is not a different type of contract. The employee keeps the same pay rules and rights as colleagues on site. The agreement governs only the remote part.

It also differs from classic telework, where the employee works from one fixed remote location. Lavoro agile is more flexible, which is why the rules must be written.

## Why it must be written

The agreement is required for administrative purposes and as proof. In practice it:

- shows that both sides agreed;
- sets the limits of the employer's control over someone working out of sight;
- supports the mandatory communication to the authorities;
- protects both sides in a dispute about hours, tools, safety or discipline.

A global remote policy written for Sweden or Denmark usually does not address the points Italian law expects.

## What it covers

**How the work is done outside the premises.** Which activities can be remote, how the employee reports and how the employer directs the work, and which technology is used.

**The employer's control.** Monitoring employees is restricted in Italy. The agreement states how supervision works and must respect the rules on remote monitoring. If you use productivity or monitoring software, check this first.

**Discipline.** Conduct outside the premises that can lead to disciplinary action, so the employee knows the rules.

**Tools.** Who provides laptop and phone, who pays maintenance, who is responsible for security, and the conditions for any personal devices.

**Rest and disconnection.** Rest periods and the technical and organisational measures that make disconnection possible. Nordic teams generally like this part.

**Duration and ending.** Open-ended or fixed term, and the notice to end the arrangement. Some employees, for example those with disabilities, have stronger protection.

**Health and safety.** The employer remains responsible. It must give the employee written information on the risks of working outside the premises, and the employee must cooperate.

## Equal treatment

A remote employee must be treated no worse than colleagues doing the same work on site, including pay under the CCNL, training and career opportunities. For a remote-first Nordic company with no Italian office this is rarely an issue, but it matters if you later open one.

## Fully remote, no office

If your Italian employee will never have an office, the agreement still applies. It simply describes a fully remote arrangement. Equipment, safety information and disconnection rules become even more important.

## Common mistakes

- Granting remote work by email.
- Using one global policy for every country.
- Skipping the right to disconnect.
- Adding monitoring tools without checking the limits.
- Forgetting the written safety information.
- Not filing the communication to the authorities.

## Steps

1. Decide which roles are remote, and how much.
2. Draft the agreement in Italian, with an English version for your managers.
3. Align it with the CCNL for the role.
4. Set availability windows and disconnection rules.
5. Define equipment and costs.
6. Hand over the safety information in writing.
7. File the communication and keep proof.

As Employer of Record (EOR), we prepare the agreement, file the communication and keep it current. You run the work.

## Questions we hear from Nordic companies

**Does a fully remote employee need an office address?**
The contract states a place of work, and the agreement describes remote work. We set both up so that the employee can work from home without an office.

**Can the employee work from another country for a while?**
Short periods abroad are usually fine. Longer periods can move tax and social security to another country. Ask us before agreeing it.

More on engineering roles in [Hire software engineers in Italy](/hire-software-engineers-italy.html). For the cost of a remote hire, try the [cost calculator](/calculator.html).

content: For many Nordic companies, the first Italian hire is a seller. That raises a question an engineering hire does not: can this person create a permanent establishment for your company in Italy, with Italian corporate tax on part of your profits? This article explains the issue in practical terms. It is not tax advice. The answer for your company depends on facts, the tax treaty between Italy and your home country, and how the role is set up. ## What a permanent establishment is In broad terms, a foreign company has a permanent establishment in a country when it has a fixed place of business there, or a person who habitually concludes contracts on its behalf, or plays the principal role leading to contracts that are routinely concluded without material changes. A permanent establishment means the company may owe local corporate tax on profits attributable to it, plus filings. An Employer of Record (EOR) makes us the employer. It does not change what the employee does for you. If the activity creates a permanent establishment, the EOR structure alone does not remove it. ## Where the risk is low - Engineering, product, support, back office and other roles that do not sell. - Marketing and pre-sales support that does not negotiate terms. - Supplier quality and sourcing roles that buy rather than sell. - Customer success for existing contracts concluded elsewhere. ## Where the risk grows - The seller negotiates prices and terms and signs contracts in your name. - The seller does everything except formally sign, and head office approves without changes. - There is an office or another fixed place at your disposal in Italy. - Italian revenue is significant and growing. ## What reduces the risk **Keep authority to conclude contracts at head office.** The Italian seller generates leads, presents and negotiates within limits. Final terms are set and approved by your Nordic team, and contracts are signed there. **Document the process.** Approval steps, pricing authority and signatories in writing. A real process is more convincing than a policy that nobody follows. **Avoid a fixed place of business.** Home-based work under a lavoro agile agreement is not the same as an office you control. Be careful with dedicated premises. **Review as you grow.** A model that is fine with one seller and modest revenue may not be with five sellers and a large Italian book. ## When an entity is the better answer If the Italian team concludes sales as its core activity, a local company or branch is often the cleaner structure. You pay Italian tax on Italian profits through a vehicle designed for it, rather than carrying uncertainty. Many Nordic companies start with an EOR seller, prove the market, and set up an entity when sales take off. ## What we do As Employer of Record, we draft the employment contract and job description so that the role is clear, including where authority to conclude contracts sits. We do not give corporate tax advice; we recommend your tax adviser reviews the set-up, and we work with them. [Review: permanent establishment wording to be validated by our labour lawyer and a tax adviser before publishing.] ## Checklist 1. Define the role: sell, support, or both? 2. Decide who negotiates and who signs. 3. Write the approval process down. 4. Avoid a fixed place of business at your disposal. 5. Review the set-up every year. ## Questions we hear from Nordic companies **Does a home office create a fixed place of business?** Generally a home office used by the employee is different from premises at your disposal, but the facts matter: who pays for it, whether it is used for customer meetings, and whether it is required by you. Discuss it with your tax adviser. **Does marketing activity count?** Activities of a preparatory or auxiliary nature are treated differently from concluding contracts. Marketing support usually belongs to that category, but keep the boundaries clear. ## In short An Italian seller is the most likely hire to create a taxable presence. Keep contract authority at head office, write down the approval process, avoid a fixed place of business at your disposal, and review the set-up as revenue grows. When Italian sales become a core business, a local company is usually the cleaner answer. See [your first seller in Italy](/hire-sales-italy.html) for the employment side, and [when to move to your own company](/articles/when-to-move-from-eor-to-italian-company.html).

A Swedish manager knows the routine. The employee reports sick, the employer pays sick pay of 80% for the first 14 calendar days, a qualifying deduction of 20% of average weekly pay is made once per period, and Försäkringskassan takes over after day 14 ([Försäkringskassan](https://www.forsakringskassan.se/arbetsgivare/sjukdom-och-skada/sjuk-medarbetare-dag-1-90/sjuklon)).

Italy works on a different logic. The certificate comes first, it goes through the state, and the employer sees much less.

## How the certificate works

In Italy the doctor issues the medical certificate electronically and sends it directly to INPS, the social security institute. The employee receives a protocol number.

The employer does not receive the diagnosis. It can see that the employee is certified unfit for work and for which period. Nothing else.

So the manager's role is narrow. You do not collect medical documents. You check that a valid certificate exists, and you plan the work.

## What the employee must do

The employee must still tell you about the absence, promptly and usually before the working day starts. Most CCNLs also expect them to share the protocol number. Put this in your onboarding material: which channel, which person. Nordic teams that are relaxed about "just post in the channel" should still name the process explicitly.

## Who pays

Sick pay in Italy is split between INPS and the employer, in proportions set by the national collective agreement (CCNL), by length of service and by type of absence. Some CCNLs require the employer to top up what INPS pays so that the employee receives close to full pay.

There is no Italian equivalent of the Swedish qualifying deduction in the standard set-up. Do not apply one by habit.

Budget this as part of the employment cost. It varies by sector, and we show it in the quote.

## What a manager can ask

- Whether the absence has been reported and through which channel.
- The certificate protocol number, so payroll can verify it.
- Whether urgent work or handovers need covering.
- The end date shown on the certificate.

And, kindly, to be told if the return date changes.

## What a manager should not ask

- **The diagnosis.** Health data is among the most protected categories under GDPR. You do not need it.
- **Symptoms.** A friendly "what do you have?" can be read as an intrusion.
- **Extra proof.** No further notes, photos or test results.
- **Whether they are really sick.** Doubts go to HR or to us, not into a chat.
- **Work during sick leave.** No emails, no "quick call". It undermines the leave and creates risk.

A simple rule: if the answer would not change how you plan the work, do not ask. Most Nordic managers already work this way. The Italian rules make it formal.

## Home checks

Italy has a system of medical control visits. During set daily time bands the employee must be reachable at the declared address. The employer can request a check, and INPS can order one, with exemptions for some conditions and appointments.

Suspicion of abuse is not a reason to confront the employee. Speak to us first. A control visit follows its own formal procedure.

## Practical steps

1. Write a short sick leave note that reflects Italian practice, not the Swedish routine.
2. Brief managers on what they can and cannot ask.
3. Name one person, or your EOR, to verify certificates and keep records.
4. Keep absence records separate from any health information, and in most cases hold no health information at all.
5. Check the CCNL for top-ups and special rules.

As Employer of Record (EOR), we retrieve the certificate data, record the absence in payroll and flag anything unusual. You plan the cover.

## Questions we hear from Nordic companies

**What if an employee is sick often?**
Do not draw conclusions from certificates. Talk about workload and wellbeing, and involve us. The CCNL sets a protected period for sickness; dismissal rules around long illness are formal and need advice.

**Does sickness during holiday count as holiday?**
Under Italian rules, illness certified during holiday can interrupt it, so the days are not lost. The employee must follow the certificate procedure.

See the sick-pay row in [Italy vs Sweden](/italy-vs-sweden.html), and the cost effect in the [cost calculator](/calculator.html).

In Stockholm, Oslo, Copenhagen and Helsinki, an employee gets twelve salaries a year. The summer bump comes from holiday pay rules, not from an extra salary. So when an Italian candidate mentions "tredicesima" and "quattordicesima", Nordic managers often hear "bonus". It is not a bonus. It is part of the agreed annual pay, paid in extra instalments.

## What they are

The **13th month** (tredicesima) is an extra instalment of salary on top of the twelve monthly payments. Every Italian national collective agreement (CCNL) provides it, and it is usually paid in December.

The **14th month** (quattordicesima) works the same way but exists only in some CCNLs, such as Commerce and services, and is usually paid in June or July.

The key point for an offer: Italian candidates negotiate a gross annual figure, the RAL. That figure already includes the 13th month and any 14th. It is divided into thirteen or fourteen parts, not twelve.

So under a 14-instalment CCNL, the monthly gross is the RAL divided by fourteen, not by twelve. Same annual pay, a smaller monthly number. Get this wrong in a conversation and the candidate thinks you are offering less than you are.

## Not discretionary

Because it is part of pay, the 13th month cannot be skipped in a weak year or tied to targets. It accrues month by month: an employee who joins in July has earned half of it by December, and an employee who leaves in March receives the share earned to that date.

Like any pay, it carries employer contributions and counts toward the TFR.

## Why the structure exists

The extra instalments come from Italian bargaining tradition and are now fixed in the CCNLs. Employees plan around them: Christmas, summer holidays, school costs, tax payments. Do not expect an Italian employee to see them as optional.

## The cash-flow problem

A Nordic finance team is used to an even payroll. With lump-sum 13th and 14th payments, Italian payroll is uneven: December and June or July are heavy months, and the employer contributions on those instalments come with them.

There is also an accounting issue. The cost builds up during the year even though the cash goes out later. If you book only when you pay, the first months look cheaper than they are and December looks expensive.

## Two ways to flatten it

**Accrue monthly.** Book one-twelfth of the annual extra instalments every month and mark the heavy months in the treasury forecast. This works if you employ through your own Italian company.

**Pay pro rata.** Where the CCNL or an individual agreement allows it, the 13th and 14th month can be paid in twelve equal parts with the monthly salary. The employee receives the same annual amount, in even payments. Your monthly cost is flat.

In our Employer of Record (EOR) quotes, the 13th and 14th month are paid pro rata in each monthly payslip by default. Combined with the TFR paid monthly into a fund, every invoice is the same size, and nothing builds up for December or for an exit.

## Talking to the candidate

Be explicit:

- state the RAL and the number of instalments;
- say whether the 13th and 14th are paid as lump sums or spread over twelve months;
- if you think in monthly salary, convert carefully and show both numbers.

Explain the structure to your own leadership too. A Nordic CFO reading an annual figure will divide by twelve unless told otherwise.

## Checklist

- Confirm the CCNL and whether it has a 14th month.
- Decide lump sum or pro rata.
- Budget on annual cost including employer contributions on the extra months.
- Include the accrued share in any exit planning.

## Questions we hear from Nordic companies

**Can we just pay twelve larger salaries instead?**
Only where the CCNL or an individual agreement allows the 13th and 14th to be paid pro rata. The annual amount stays the same; what changes is the timing. We check the agreement before proposing it, and we write the choice into the contract so the payslips are consistent from the first month.

**Does the 13th month count for holiday pay or the TFR?**
It counts toward the TFR, like other regular pay. Holiday in Italy is paid as normal salary while the employee is off, so there is no separate holiday-pay percentage to apply on top, which is a common double count in Nordic models.

**What happens if the employee leaves in October?**
They receive the share of the 13th (and any 14th) accrued to the leaving date in the final payslip. If the extra months were paid pro rata, most of it has already been paid and the final settlement is smaller.

The [cost calculator](/calculator.html) shows the twelve invoices both ways. For other pay differences, see [Italy vs Sweden](/italy-vs-sweden.html).

Sweden and Finland have strong vehicle, truck, bus and component industries. Turin has been the centre of Italian automotive engineering for more than a century. When a Nordic company needs engineers who know Italian suppliers, Italian testing practice or simply Europe's second automotive tradition, Turin is the first place to look.

## What the talent pool looks like

Turin and Piedmont offer:

- vehicle engineering, powertrain and chassis specialists from the long presence of large car makers and their suppliers;
- electrical and electronic engineers working on electrification, battery systems and vehicle software;
- aerospace and space systems engineers;
- industrial automation and manufacturing engineers;
- a growing ICT and software sector.

The Politecnico di Torino trains mechanical, aerospace, electronic and computer engineers, and the Università di Torino adds sciences and economics. Many senior engineers have spent years inside large industrial groups and know how suppliers, homologation and quality systems work.

## Why it fits Nordic companies

- **Supplier proximity.** Many Nordic OEMs and tier-one suppliers buy from Italian component makers. An engineer in Turin can manage supplier quality, development and launches on the spot.
- **Electrification.** The overlap between Nordic electrification programmes and Piedmontese engineering is growing.
- **Same time zone** as Gothenburg and Stockholm, one hour from Helsinki.
- **Lower cost than Milan**, with comparable engineering depth.

## Local income tax

Employees in Turin pay the national IRPEF plus regional and municipal surcharges. Turin is unusual: its city surcharge is progressive, in four brackets of 0.8%, 0.8%, 1.1% and 1.2%, with an exemption threshold of €11,790 (pmi.it, 730/2026 table, secondary source). The Piedmont regional surcharge starts at 1.62% up to €15,000, with increases planned for 2026 to 2028.

For a senior engineer, the city surcharge in Turin is somewhat higher than in Milan or Bologna at the same gross. Lower housing costs usually more than offset it. It changes net pay, not your employer cost.

## The usual contract

Engineering roles in this sector normally fall under the Metalworking agreement (CCNL Metalmeccanico industria). It sets levels, pay tables, travel rules, shift premiums and a supplementary health fund. Employer contributions are a little higher than under Commerce and services, and INAIL injury insurance is higher for technical roles than for office ones.

## Practical points

- **Travel.** Supplier and plant visits are part of most roles. The CCNL governs travel allowances and travel time.
- **Trips to Sweden or Finland.** Training at your plant is a business trip. Longer assignments need a posting notification; we handle it.
- **Safety training.** Required before site visits.
- **Confidentiality and IP.** Our contracts assign inventions and designs to your company.
- **Senior roles.** Experienced engineers can be hired at "quadro" level.

## Hiring without an Italian entity

With an Employer of Record (EOR), we employ the engineer in Italy under the right CCNL and run payroll, while your engineering organisation manages the work. Cost: the employment cost plus €250 a month, invoiced in SEK or EUR.

## Questions we hear from Nordic companies

**Can the engineer work on our programmes from Turin full time?**
Yes. Many work remotely on Nordic programmes with regular trips to suppliers and to your sites. The working-time and travel rules of the CCNL apply.

**Are Turin engineers used to English?**
Engineers from international programmes and large suppliers usually work in English daily. Check during the interview, as you would anywhere.

**What about security clearance or export control?**
If the work involves controlled technology, check export-control rules with your compliance team before hiring. The employment structure does not change those obligations.

**Can we hire a team, not one engineer?**
Yes. Several engineers in Turin can be employed through the EOR under the same CCNL, each with their own contract, and managed as one team from your organisation.

## In short

Turin offers Nordic vehicle and component makers deep engineering experience at a lower cost than Milan, in the same time zone. Hire under the Metalworking CCNL, write travel and IP terms into the contract, and remember that the progressive city surcharge affects the net pay of senior engineers. Through an EOR the engineer can start within days for EU citizens, managed entirely by your engineering organisation.

See the [Turin city page](/hire-in-turin.html) and the [industrial engineers page](/hire-engineers-manufacturing-italy.html). Estimate a salary in the [cost calculator](/calculator.html).

Nordic employers work with unions as a matter of course. In Sweden, wages are set through collective bargaining between unions and employers' organisations at sector and company level, and agreements cover close to 90% of employees ([Medlingsinstitutet](https://www.mi.se/app/uploads/the-swedish-model-and-collective-agreements.pdf)). Local negotiation and information duties are part of normal management, and Danish, Norwegian and Finnish companies have similar traditions.

So a Nordic company hiring in Italy often asks: will we have to negotiate with Italian unions? For a small team, the honest answer is: rarely directly, but always indirectly.

## Unions through the CCNL

Italian unions' main influence on a small employer is the national collective agreement (CCNL). Unions and employer associations negotiate it for each sector, and it sets pay floors, levels, hours, leave, notice and much more. When you apply the CCNL, you apply what the unions negotiated.

That is the indirect presence: every Italian employee's terms already reflect union bargaining, even if nobody in your team is a member.

## Membership

Italian employees are free to join a union, and the employer must respect that. Union dues are deducted through payroll for members who ask. You should not ask candidates or employees about membership, just as you would not at home.

## Workplace representation

In larger Italian workplaces, employees can elect workplace union representatives, with rights to information, meetings and paid time for union activity. Thresholds and procedures depend on the law and the CCNL. A small, distributed team employed through an EOR will normally not have workplace representation. As you grow, and especially if you open your own Italian company with a larger team, expect it.

## When unions appear in a small team

- **Disputes.** An employee who disagrees with a decision may seek support from a union, which can advise and represent them.
- **Settlements.** Agreed exits are often signed in a protected setting, which can include a union venue, so that the agreement is final.
- **Collective dismissals.** Procedures with union consultation apply above certain thresholds.
- **CCNL renewals.** When a CCNL is renewed, new pay tables apply to your employees automatically.

## Differences from Nordic practice

- **Less local bargaining.** In a small Italian team you will rarely negotiate locally the way a Swedish company does with a local union club.
- **Less information duty in daily management.** Nordic co-determination habits are good practice, but small Italian employers do not normally have the same formal consultation duties on everyday decisions.
- **More formal disputes.** When conflicts arise, they move to a formal setting faster than in a Nordic workplace.

## Good practice

Keep your Nordic instincts: transparency, early information, treating representatives as partners. They work well in Italy and build trust. Add the Italian formal frame: written decisions, correct procedures and the right CCNL.

As Employer of Record (EOR), we apply the CCNL and its renewals, handle union dues in payroll and manage any formal contact. You keep a direct, open relationship with your team.

## Questions we hear from Nordic companies

**Do we need to inform unions when we hire?**
No, not for individual hires in a small team. Hiring is notified to the labour authorities electronically, which we do as employer.

**Can an employee bring a union representative to a disciplinary meeting?**
The disciplinary procedure gives the employee the right to respond, and they can be assisted by a union representative. Plan for it and keep the procedure formal.

**What happens when a CCNL is renewed?**
New pay tables and terms apply from the dates in the agreement, sometimes with back pay. We apply them and show the effect on your cost before the invoice.

**Will Italian employees expect co-determination like in Sweden?**
Not as a legal process in a small team, but they will appreciate being informed early about changes that affect them. That habit costs nothing and pays back in trust.

## In short

For a small Nordic employer in Italy, unions are present mainly through the CCNL, which you apply to every employee. Workplace representation and local bargaining come with size. Respect membership, follow formal procedures in disputes, and apply CCNL renewals on time. Nordic habits of transparency and early information work well and build trust.

For how CCNLs compare with Nordic agreements, see [Italian CCNL vs Swedish kollektivavtal](/articles/italy-ccnl-vs-swedish-collective-agreements.html) and [Italy vs Sweden](/italy-vs-sweden.html).

An Employer of Record (EOR) is a way to start, not always a way to stay. Many Nordic companies use an EOR for their first Italian hires and later set up an Italian srl or a branch. The question is when.

There is no single headcount that answers it. The answer depends on what the Italian team does and how stable the plan is.

## Signals that it is time

**The team is large and stable.** With several employees and a multi-year plan, the fixed costs of an Italian company are spread over enough people.

**Italian staff sell and sign in your name.** If your Italian employees regularly negotiate and conclude contracts with Italian customers, you may create a permanent establishment for tax purposes. At that point a local company or branch is often the cleaner structure.

**You need a legal presence.** Public tenders, certain licences, product registrations, or customers who require an Italian counterparty.

**You want an office.** Leasing premises, local bank accounts and supplier contracts are simpler with your own entity.

**Group policy.** Some Nordic groups require their own entity once a country passes a certain size or revenue.

## Signals that it is not yet time

- The plan is still uncertain.
- The team is small or distributed across Italy.
- Staff do engineering, support or back-office work rather than local sales.
- You expect to expand into other countries next and prefer one model for all of them.

## What setting up involves

An Italian srl or branch requires incorporation, a bank account, registration with the tax agency, INPS and INAIL, a payroll provider or in-house payroll, an accountant, statutory accounts and annual filings. It takes months, and the costs stay even if the team shrinks.

Plan it as a project: legal set-up, payroll set-up, accounting, and only then employee transfer.

## How employees move

The transfer is a change of employer, not a new hire. Done properly:

- seniority is kept;
- the CCNL and level normally stay the same;
- accrued holiday and hours off are carried over or settled;
- the TFR either moves or has already been paid monthly into the employee's pension fund, which makes the transfer simpler.

The employees sign with the new company, and we close our contracts on the same date. No gap, no new probation.

## Running payroll after the move

You can run payroll yourself, use a local provider, or keep us: we run payroll for Italian entities at €55 per payslip, with the same team your employees already know.

## A hybrid model

Some companies keep the EOR for new cities or roles while the entity covers the core team. This is common when the Italian company is in Milan and new hires are remote elsewhere.

## Questions to ask

1. How many people will we have in Italy in two years?
2. Do they conclude contracts with Italian customers?
3. Do we need an Italian legal counterparty?
4. Who will run payroll and accounts?
5. How certain is the plan?

## Questions we hear from Nordic companies

**Can we keep some employees on the EOR after setting up the company?**
Yes. A hybrid model is common, especially for remote employees in other cities or for roles you are still testing.

**Do employees need to agree to the transfer?**
They sign a new contract with your company. In practice, with seniority and terms preserved, most employees welcome the move. Communicate early and clearly.

**What happens to the probation period after the transfer?**
None is needed. The employee keeps their seniority, so a new probation period would not be appropriate. Confirm this in the transfer documents.

## In short

Move to your own Italian company when the team is large and stable, when Italian staff conclude sales, or when you need a legal presence. Stay with an EOR while the plan is uncertain or the team is small and distributed. Plan the entity as a project, transfer the employees with their seniority, and decide who will run payroll before the first transfer date. A hybrid model is often the practical middle ground.

For the comparison of models, see [EOR, own company or freelancers](/italy-eor-vs-entity.html). For pricing of both services, see [pricing](/pricing.html).

A US company hiring in Italy fights the time zone. A Nordic company does not. Stockholm, Oslo, Copenhagen and Milan share the same clock; Helsinki is one hour ahead. Stand-ups, lunch and the Friday wrap-up line up by default.

That removes the biggest source of friction, but not all of it. Italian working time is more regulated in writing than Nordic managers expect, and the informal flexibility common in Nordic tech teams needs a written frame in Italy.

## The frame: law plus CCNL

The normal working week in Italy is 40 hours, and the average including overtime cannot exceed 48 hours. Many national collective agreements (CCNLs) set fewer normal hours. The CCNL also decides:

- how the normal week is scheduled;
- what counts as overtime and how it is paid;
- daily breaks;
- night, weekend and holiday work;
- whether extra hours can be banked as time off.

Before you agree a schedule, read the working-time chapter of the CCNL that applies to the role.

## Overtime is a category, not a favour

In many Nordic companies, salaried staff on trust-based working time simply absorb a busy week and take it back later. In Italy, overtime is defined and tracked. It usually needs to be requested or authorised, recorded, and compensated the way the CCNL says: extra pay, a premium, or time off in lieu.

Three habits help:

1. Approve overtime before it happens, in writing, even in a short message.
2. Record the hours; do not rely on memory at month end.
3. Tell the employee in advance how extra hours will be compensated.

For senior engineers and managers, an Italian contract can be set up at "quadro" level with a flat arrangement for extra hours. Ask us when that fits.

## Rest is protected

Italian law gives weight to rest between working days and to weekly rest. A late release that runs to midnight followed by an early meeting is a compliance issue, not just a courtesy issue. Plan the next day when someone works late.

## The right to disconnect

Italy recognises disconnection mainly in remote work (lavoro agile). The written remote-work agreement sets rest periods and the measures that make disconnection real. Nordic teams already value this; the difference is that it must be written down.

Short, practical norms are enough:

- define core hours when the employee is reachable;
- messages outside those hours need no answer until the next working period;
- do not reward or punish out-of-hours responsiveness;
- use scheduled send for late-evening messages.

## Where Nordic habits need adjusting

**Flexitime without records.** Many Nordic employees run flexible hours on trust. In Italy you still need a record of hours, especially for roles that are not at manager level.

**Summer hours.** Some Nordic companies shorten the day in summer. That is fine in Italy too, but it changes the contractual hours. Put it in writing as a company policy.

**Different holiday calendars.** Midsummer and the Nordic July slowdown do not exist in Italy. Italian public holidays and the August slowdown do not exist at home. Keep a shared calendar.

**Helsinki and Reykjavik.** Finnish teams are one hour ahead; Icelandic teams one hour behind in winter and two in summer. Put recurring meetings inside the shared window.

## Put it on one page

A short working-time note attached to the employment documents prevents most conflicts. It should cover core hours, how overtime is approved and paid, and the disconnection norm. Predictable hours also mean predictable overtime cost.

As Employer of Record (EOR), we check the CCNL rules for the role so that your note matches what the contract requires.

## Questions we hear from Nordic companies

**Can we use trust-based working time as at home?**
For managers and some senior roles a more flexible arrangement is possible under the CCNL. For most roles, working time must be recorded. We advise per role.

**Are we liable if an employee chooses to work late?**
If you know about it and benefit from it, it can be treated as overtime. Make the approval rule clear and follow it.

For other differences, see [Italy vs Sweden](/italy-vs-sweden.html). To price a role, use the [cost calculator](/calculator.html).
